title: Cross-cutting senior scenarios (Kotlin + Coroutines + Flow)
scopeHtml: All questions in this chunk are SCENARIO questions that deliberately combine Kotlin language features, coroutines, and Flow in realistic production settings.

questions.contextHtml: You own the search screen of a shopping app: 2M DAU, ~9 searches per session, p95 backend latency 450 ms on 4G, 18% of users on low-end devices (2 GB RAM, API 26-28). Product wants "search as you type", recent searches shown when the field is empty, results that survive rotation and process death of the query text, and no stale results ever shown for an older query. Crashlytics currently shows 0.4% of search sessions with "results flicker back to old query" and the backend team complains search QPS is 6x what it was before the type-ahead launch. The current code launches viewModelScope.launch { repo.search(text) } from a TextWatcher on every keystroke.
questions.promptHtml: Design the search pipeline end to end, from the text field to the rendered list. Name every operator and scope choice and defend it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use debounce and flatMapLatest." Stops there. Cannot say where the query state lives, what happens on process death, how empty/short queries are handled, how errors avoid killing the pipeline, or why collectLatest in the UI is not a substitute for flatMapLatest in the ViewModel.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Min query length (backend rejects < 2 chars?). Do results need to be cached per query? Is the endpoint idempotent and cancel-safe (does the server bill per request)? Should "enter/search" key bypass the debounce? Is there a recent-searches store (Room/DataStore) I must merge?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but the QPS regression is real. I would first put a 250-300 ms debounce and a distinctUntilChanged in front of the call, behind a remote flag, because that alone cuts QPS roughly by the average burst length (e.g. 9 keystrokes per word into ~2 calls).
  3. Hypotheses (for the flicker bug), ranked: (a) responses arrive out of order and last-writer-wins on the UI state; (b) two collectors are active after rotation; (c) a cached result for an older query is emitted after the new one; (d) the Retrofit call is not cancelled, so a late response still writes state.
  4. How I'd verify: Log query + request id + arrival order in a debug build; replay with a throttled proxy (Charles/Network Link Conditioner); a unit test with runTest and a fake repo that delays the first query longer than the second.
  5. Root cause: Independent launch per keystroke means no ordering guarantee. Cancellation is the only thing that makes "newest wins" true, and nothing was cancelling.
  6. Fix: One pipeline, one state owner:
class SearchViewModel(
    private val repo: SearchRepository,
    private val saved: SavedStateHandle,
) : ViewModel() {

    private val query = saved.getMutableStateFlow("q", "")   // survives process death (lifecycle-viewmodel-savedstate 2.5+)

    val state: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = query
        .map { it.trim() }
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .debounce { if (it.isEmpty()) 0L else 300L }          // clear is instant, typing is debounced
        .flatMapLatest { q ->
            when {
                q.isEmpty() -> repo.recentSearches().map { SearchUiState.Recent(it) }
                q.length < 2 -> flowOf(SearchUiState.TooShort)
                else -> flow {
                    emit(SearchUiState.Loading(q))
                    emit(SearchUiState.Results(q, repo.search(q)))   // suspend, cancel-safe
                }.catch { e ->
                    if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                    emit(SearchUiState.Error(q, e))
                }
            }
        }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState.Recent(emptyList()))

    fun onQueryChanged(text: String) { query.value = text }
}

debounce { } with a lambda timeout is @FlowPreview in kotlinx.coroutines 1.8-1.10; I would opt in explicitly and note that. getMutableStateFlow exists on SavedStateHandle from lifecycle-viewmodel-savedstate 2.5. 7. Prevention: a runTest test using virtual time: type "ab", advance 100 ms, type "abc", advance 300 ms, assert exactly one repo call with "abc". A second test where call 1 takes 1000 ms and call 2 takes 100 ms and the final state is always for call 2. Lint: ban viewModelScope.launch inside TextWatcher/onValueChange handlers via code review checklist. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use collectLatest in the UI as the cancellation mechanism: the repo call would already be running upstream, and the cancellation point would only be the render step. I would not put catch after stateIn (it cannot restart the upstream). I would not use conflate() here: it drops intermediate emissions but does not cancel in-flight work. Debounce costs 300 ms of perceived latency; mitigate with an immediate local-prefix suggestion from Room FTS while the network call is pending. flatMapLatest is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi and I accept that, as it has been stable in practice for years.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "User hits the search key; should the debounce wait?" → No. Merge a second Channel<String>/SharedFlow of "submit" events via merge ahead of the debounce, or use debounce { if (it.submitted) 0 else 300 } with a small wrapper type.
  • "Backend returns 429 under load." → Catch inside the inner flow so the outer pipeline survives; map to Error, retry with backoff only on explicit user action, never auto-retry inside flatMapLatest because every new keystroke already re-issues.
  • "Why not shareIn?" → I need the latest value for new subscribers (rotation), so stateIn; WhileSubscribed(5_000) survives rotation without restarting the query.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A type-ahead launch tripled backend QPS in a day; the team added debounce and the flicker bug disappeared as a side effect, which hid that cancellation was still missing. Two weeks later a slow-network cohort reproduced the exact out-of-order bug. The fix that stuck was making the ordering guarantee structural (flatMapLatest), not timing-based.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: per-keystroke launch, or only "debounce" with no ordering/cancellation story.
  • Hire: debounce + distinctUntilChanged + flatMapLatest + StateFlow, handles errors inside the inner flow.
  • Strong hire: adds SavedStateHandle, empty/short-query branches, WhileSubscribed rationale, cancellation-safe catch, virtual-time tests, and explains why collectLatest/conflate are not substitutes.

questions.contextHtml:
Fintech app, 800K DAU. Access tokens live 15 minutes. After a backend change that shortened them from 60 to 15 minutes, support tickets spike: users are randomly logged out. Logs on the auth server show bursts of 6-12 POST /oauth/refresh calls within 200 ms from the same device, with the same refresh token. The auth server uses rotating refresh tokens (each refresh token is single-use), so only the first succeeds; the rest get 400 invalid_grant, and the app treats that as "session expired" and logs the user out. Your app fires up to 8 parallel requests on the home screen. Client code in an OkHttp Authenticator:

class TokenAuthenticator(private val auth: AuthRepository) : Authenticator {
    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        val newToken = runBlocking { auth.refresh() }   // suspend, hits network
        return response.request.newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer $newToken")
            .build()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain exactly why this fails, fix it so exactly one refresh happens per expiry, and discuss the failure modes of your fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized." Without comparing the token on the failed request, the second thread still refreshes again (with an already-rotated token). Or "don't use runBlocking" without noting that Authenticator.authenticate is a blocking Java API, so blocking is unavoidable at that boundary.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are refresh tokens rotating and single-use (yes, per the logs)? Is there a grace window on the server for reuse? How are tokens persisted (EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore)? Does the app have multiple processes? What must happen on a true invalid_grant vs a network failure during refresh?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side: add a 10-30 s reuse grace window if the auth team can. Client hotfix: do not log out on invalid_grant unless the stored refresh token equals the one we sent. That alone stops the user-visible logouts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) N parallel 401s each enter authenticate and each calls refresh; (b) a second refresh happens after the first finished because the late 401 responses carry an old token; (c) token store is read non-atomically; (d) a proactive interceptor also refreshes.
  4. How I'd verify: OkHttp HttpLoggingInterceptor at HEADERS with redactHeader("Authorization") plus a request-id; count refresh calls per 401 burst in a test using MockWebServer with a dispatcher that returns 401 until a new token is used; check the server log for the single-use violations.
  5. Root cause: authenticate is invoked concurrently on OkHttp dispatcher threads. Each one sees a 401 and calls refresh. With single-use rotation, race losers get invalid_grant, which the app mis-maps to "logged out".
  6. Fix: serialize and de-duplicate by comparing the token that failed with the current one:
class TokenAuthenticator(private val store: TokenStore, private val api: AuthApi) : Authenticator {
    private val mutex = Mutex()   // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex; not reentrant

    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        if (responseCount(response) >= 2) return null            // give up, avoid infinite loop
        val failedToken = response.request.header("Authorization")?.removePrefix("Bearer ")
        return runBlocking {                                      // OkHttp thread, not Main
            mutex.withLock {
                val current = store.accessToken()
                val token = if (current != null && current != failedToken) {
                    current                                       // someone else already refreshed
                } else {
                    try { api.refresh(store.refreshToken()).also { store.save(it) }.accessToken }
                    catch (e: HttpException) { if (e.code() == 400) store.clearIfSame(store.refreshToken()); return@runBlocking null }
                }
                response.request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $token").build()
            }
        }
    }
    private fun responseCount(r: Response): Int = generateSequence(r) { it.priorResponse }.count()
}

Key: runBlocking here is acceptable because authenticate is a blocking contract running on an OkHttp thread; what is not acceptable is calling it on Main. Mutex vs synchronized: either works; Mutex lets the refresh body itself be suspending without pinning inside a monitor. 7. Prevention: a MockWebServer concurrency test (8 parallel calls, expect 1 refresh); metric on refresh count per session; alert when invalid_grant rate exceeds baseline; never clear credentials on a transient error (timeouts, 5xx). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a CompletableDeferred shared "in-flight refresh" without the token comparison (late 401s would start a second refresh). Not proactive refresh via timer alone (clock skew, backgrounded process). I'd still add a proactive refresh 60 s before expiry as an optimization, with the same mutex. Multi-process: Mutex is per-process; use a single auth process or file lock if you really have several.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not suspend in authenticate?" → The interface is a Java blocking SAM; Retrofit's suspend support sits above it. You bridge with runBlocking at that boundary only.
  • "Refresh itself returns 401?" → responseCount guard plus the refresh call must use a client without this authenticator, otherwise recursion.
  • "User cancels the screen mid-refresh?" → The Retrofit coroutine is cancelled, but the Authenticator's refresh runs on OkHttp's thread and completes, which is desirable: the token still gets saved.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" the logouts by adding synchronized and saw them drop 80%, not 100%. The remaining 20% were late 401s from slow responses carrying the pre-refresh token: each one acquired the lock after the refresh and refreshed again. The token comparison was the missing piece.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the backend, or adds a lock without the compare check.
  • Hire: mutex + compare failed token vs stored token, loop guard.
  • Strong hire: also handles invalid_grant semantics, runBlocking justification, separate client for refresh, MockWebServer concurrency test, multi-process caveat.

questions.contextHtml:
Payments screen, "Pay Now" button. Over a weekend, 312 customers (0.09% of 340K payments) were charged twice. Timeline: the payment endpoint p95 jumped from 600 ms to 3.8 s after a gateway issue. Users double-tapped because nothing happened. Code:

fun onPayClicked() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = Loading
        val result = runCatching { repo.pay(orderId, amount) }
        _state.value = result.fold({ Success }, { Error(it) })
    }
}

Backend log excerpt: two POST /pay with different X-Request-Id, 180 ms apart, same orderId, both processed.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review. What failed at each layer (UI, ViewModel, coroutines, network, server), and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable the button." That is one layer, and it fails after process death/retry, rotation, and OkHttp's retryOnConnectionFailure. Also misses that runCatching swallows CancellationException.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the server support an idempotency key? Is orderId unique per attempt or per order? Does the HTTP client auto-retry POSTs? Were any of the doubles from a retry after timeout rather than a double-tap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server: reject a second payment on an order already PAID/PENDING (unique constraint on order + attempt). Client hotfix: ignore clicks while a payment job is active. Refund the 312 and reconcile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two coroutines launched by two taps; (b) button disabled via state that updates asynchronously (StateFlow collected a frame later); (c) OkHttp retried on connection failure (default retryOnConnectionFailure = true) after a timed-out first attempt; (d) user re-entered the screen after process death while the first request was still in flight.
  4. How I'd verify: Tap-spam UI test with Espresso/Compose test (performClick() twice with idling); server logs correlate request ids to the same user session; check whether the second request had Retry markers; check OkHttp client config.
  5. Root cause: No single-flight guard at the ViewModel and no idempotency key across the wire. launch per click is fire-and-forget; the Loading state is set inside the coroutine, after the launch returns, so a second click in the same frame sees the old state.
  6. Fix (layered):
private var payJob: Job? = null
private val paymentAttemptKey: String =
    savedStateHandle["attempt"] ?: UUID.randomUUID().toString().also { savedStateHandle["attempt"] = it }

fun onPayClicked() {
    if (payJob?.isActive == true) return            // synchronous guard, main thread only
    _state.value = Loading                           // set BEFORE launch returns
    payJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = try {
            repo.pay(orderId, amount, idempotencyKey = paymentAttemptKey)
            Success
        } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
        catch (e: Exception) { Error(e) }
    }
}

The key is generated once per checkout attempt, stored in SavedStateHandle so it survives process death, and sent as an Idempotency-Key header, so any retry (user, OkHttp, process restore) maps to the same server operation. New key only after a definitive failure the user chooses to retry. 7. Prevention: server-side idempotency table with TTL; client integration test that fires 2 concurrent pay() calls and asserts one backend hit; code-review rule: any money-moving endpoint requires an idempotency key; UI: disable and show progress in the same frame; do not rely on UI disabling for correctness. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just debounce clicks (a time window is a guess). Not Mutex.withLock alone (it serializes, so the second pay would still run afterwards). Not Channel-based single worker for this one button; overkill. OkHttp retryOnConnectionFailure(false) for POSTs is an option but loses resilience; idempotency key makes retries safe, so keep retries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "App is killed during the request; user reopens." → Persisted attempt key + a GET /payments?key= status check on launch before offering "Pay" again.
  • "Why not StateFlow.update with compareAndSet for the guard?" → Good for state atomicity but launch is the side effect; the Job reference or an AtomicBoolean is the guard. Main-thread-confined Job? is fine because clicks are on Main.
  • "runCatching problem?" → It catches CancellationException; if the VM scope is cancelled, you would report an Error state or continue, breaking structured cancellation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first fix shipped was a 500 ms click debounce. It passed QA and failed in production on slow phones where the second tap landed 700 ms later. Only the idempotency key closed the hole, because the retry source was often the network stack, not the user.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "disable the button".
  • Hire: Job guard in the VM + idempotency key + mentions server-side check.
  • Strong hire: identifies state-set-timing and runCatching/cancellation issues, OkHttp retry, process death persistence, and proposes tests plus a review rule.

questions.contextHtml:
Media app, 1.5M DAU. After release 7.12, Play Console shows ANR rate 0.31% -> 1.1% (bad-behavior threshold is 0.47% per the Android vitals docs). Top ANR trace (main thread):

"main" tid=1 Waiting
  at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park / java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park
  at kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking(Builders.kt)
  at kotlinx.coroutines.BuildersKt__BuildersKt.runBlocking(Builders.kt)
  at com.app.net.HeaderInterceptor.intercept(HeaderInterceptor.kt:22)
  at okhttp3.internal.http.RealInterceptorChain.proceed
  at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall.execute
  at com.app.legacy.AdLoader.fetchSync(AdLoader.java:88)

HeaderInterceptor does val flags = runBlocking { featureFlags.snapshot() } where snapshot() does withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { ... } (plain Main, not immediate). It is used by every OkHttp call.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure mechanically, give a mitigation you can ship today, and the proper fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Never use runBlocking." True but empty. Does not explain why it deadlocks only on some paths (a coroutine dispatched back to Main from a blocked Main) or why most calls "work" (enqueue path runs on OkHttp threads).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which call sites invoke execute() on main (legacy)? Is the ANR always fetchSync? What does snapshot() need from Main? Device/OS skew? Did 7.12 introduce the interceptor or the Main.immediate hop?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-config or remote kill-switch for AdLoader.fetchSync main-thread usage; hotfix HeaderInterceptor to read an in-memory @Volatile cached flags object (no coroutine at all). Ship as patch release, staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) deadlock: main thread blocked in runBlocking waiting for a continuation that must resume on Main; (b) disk/IO blocking on main (strict-mode); (c) OkHttp per-host limit (5) starvation; (d) lock contention in the flags store.
  4. How I'd verify: The trace itself shows runBlocking on main; confirm by StrictMode.detectNetwork() and detectDiskReads() in debug; reproduce by calling fetchSync from a button; check the coroutine dump (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() from kotlinx-coroutines-debug) to see a coroutine suspended waiting for Main. Grep for execute() call sites.
  5. Root cause: runBlocking on Main creates an event loop that blocks the calling thread until the block completes. The block does withContext(Dispatchers.Main); plain Main always posts to the Looper (isDispatchNeeded is true), but the Looper thread is the very thread parked inside runBlocking, so the posted continuation can never run: a classic self-deadlock, ending when the 5 s input-dispatch timeout raises the ANR. Had it been Main.immediate, isDispatchNeeded would be false on the main thread and the block would run inline (no deadlock, but Main is still blocked for the read). Deadlock only happens on the execute()-on-Main path; on OkHttp worker threads the same code just works, which is why it passed testing. Even the "working" path blocks the caller thread.
  6. Fix:
class HeaderInterceptor(private val flags: FeatureFlagCache) : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response =
        chain.proceed(chain.request().newBuilder()
            .header("X-Flags", flags.current.encoded)   // plain volatile read, no suspension
            .build())
}
class FeatureFlagCache(scope: CoroutineScope, source: FlagSource) {
    @Volatile var current: Flags = Flags.DEFAULT; private set
    init { scope.launch { source.updates().collect { current = it } } }
}

Long term: delete the sync execute() on main (move AdLoader to a suspend Retrofit call with withContext), never use runBlocking in library/network code except at a true blocking boundary on a background thread. 7. Prevention: StrictMode in debug + CI; a detekt/lint rule flagging runBlocking outside main()/tests/known boundaries (detekt has RunBlocking-style checks in coroutines ruleset, e.g. GlobalCoroutineUsage; I would add a custom rule or ban via forbidden-method-call); Play Console ANR alert at 0.35%; macrobenchmark startup trace. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrapping in withTimeout inside runBlocking (still blocks Main up to the timeout, converts deadlock into a 2 s jank). Not switching to Dispatchers.Default in snapshot() as the only fix (fixes this deadlock, keeps Main blocked). Not runBlocking(Dispatchers.IO) on main either: no deadlock, but still blocks Main.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why is runBlocking fine inside Authenticator?" → That thread is an OkHttp worker and the interface is blocking; Main is never held.
  • "Does Dispatchers.Main.immediate guarantee no dispatch?" → Only if you are already on Main; otherwise it dispatches normally. It avoids an extra post, it does not make blocking safe.
  • "How does OkHttp's enqueue path differ?" → Interceptors run on OkHttp's dispatcher threads, so Main isn't blocked; execute() runs interceptors on the caller thread.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The interceptor had shipped weeks earlier without incident because 99% of calls went through Retrofit suspend (enqueue). One legacy ad SDK wrapper used execute() on Main, and a Main-bound flag read finally made the latent deadlock hit on a specific release train.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "increase timeout" or "use coroutines".
  • Hire: explains Main blocked by runBlocking waiting for a Main-dispatched continuation; removes runBlocking.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes enqueue vs execute thread model, gives a safe cached-flag design, StrictMode/lint prevention, and ANR threshold awareness.

questions.contextHtml: Field-service app: technicians log jobs offline (up to 8 hours with no signal), 40K devices, ~150 writes per device per day, 20% on flaky 2G. Today each write does api.post() and shows a Toast on failure; ~3% of writes are silently lost. Requirements: no data loss, order per entity preserved, retries with backoff, survive process death and reboot, show per-item "pending/failed" in the UI, battery-friendly, and conflicts resolved server-wins on version mismatch.
questions.promptHtml: Design the sync engine. Where do coroutines, Flow and Kotlin types fit, and what do you delegate to the platform?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Retry in a loop with delay." Loses work on process death, retries forever on 4xx, burns battery, and has no ordering or idempotency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering required per entity or globally? Are writes idempotent (client-generated UUIDs)? Max payload and attachment sizes? Is there a delta/pull API with versions? How long can a write stay pending before the user must be told?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the silent loss: persist every mutation to Room before any network call (transactional outbox), show pending state. That gets us 0% loss even before retries are perfect.
  3. Hypotheses (for the 3% loss), ranked: process killed mid-request; failure only Toasted; 4xx treated as retriable or vice versa; no persistence of intent.
  4. How I'd verify: Fault-injection test (airplane mode mid-write, kill process), server-side count vs client-side count reconciliation, analytics funnel for "write created -> acked".
  5. Design:
UI -> Repository.save() -> Room (entity + OutboxEntry{id, entityId, payload, attempt, state, createdAt}) in ONE transaction
                               |
                      WorkManager (unique work, NetworkType.CONNECTED, exponential backoff)
                               |
                      SyncWorker (CoroutineWorker): loop over outbox grouped by entityId
                               |  per-entity sequential, entities in parallel (limit 4)
                      API with Idempotency-Key = outbox id
                               |
                      success -> delete outbox row + update entity version (transaction)
                      409 -> pull latest, server wins, mark conflict, notify
                      4xx (non-409/429) -> state=FAILED_PERMANENT, surface to user
                      5xx/IO/429 -> Result.retry() / next attempt with backoff
class SyncWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters, private val dao: OutboxDao, private val api: Api) :
    CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = coroutineScope {
        val groups = dao.pending().groupBy { it.entityId }
        val sem = Semaphore(4)
        val outcomes = groups.values.map { entries ->
            async { sem.withPermit { pushInOrder(entries) } }   // sequential inside, parallel across
        }.awaitAll()
        if (outcomes.any { it == Outcome.RETRY }) Result.retry() else Result.success()
    }

    private suspend fun pushInOrder(entries: List<OutboxEntry>): Outcome {
        for (e in entries) {
            when (val r = runCatching { api.push(e.payload, idempotencyKey = e.id) }.also { it.exceptionOrNull()?.let { t -> if (t is CancellationException) throw t } }.toOutcome()) {
                Outcome.OK -> dao.complete(e.id)
                Outcome.PERMANENT -> { dao.markFailed(e.id); return Outcome.PERMANENT }  // block later entries for that entity
                Outcome.RETRY -> return Outcome.RETRY
            }
        }
        return Outcome.OK
    }
}

Flow's role: dao.observeOutboxCounts(): Flow<Map<State, Int>> drives the "3 pending / 1 failed" UI; Room emits on table invalidation. Sealed Outcome and when exhaustiveness keep retry policy explicit. CoroutineWorker runs on Dispatchers.Default by default and cancellation is delivered when WorkManager stops it, so each push is cancellation-safe: the row is deleted only after the server ack, and the idempotency key makes a re-send harmless. 6. Fix path (rollout): Add the outbox behind a flag, dual-write for a release, compare server counts, then remove the old path. 7. Prevention: instrumentation test with WorkManagerTestInitHelper; chaos tests (kill process between push and local complete); metrics: outbox age p95, failed-permanent count, retries per item; alert if oldest pending > 24 h. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a coroutine retry loop in viewModelScope (dies with the process). Not GlobalScope / foreground service for all syncing (battery, background limits). Not unbounded parallelism (2G radio, server load). Not "last write wins" silently; conflicts must be visible. WorkManager periodic floor is 15 minutes; for immediate sync after a write enqueue one-time expedited-or-normal work with a network constraint. Expedited work has quotas, so don't depend on it for correctness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Order across entities (job depends on customer)?" → Add dependsOn to outbox rows; the worker skips entries whose dependency is not yet acked.
  • "100K pending rows after 3 days offline?" → Page the pending query (LIMIT 200), batch endpoint, and keep the worker under WorkManager's ~10 minute execution limit by returning Result.retry() with progress persisted.
  • "How do you make the UI show truth immediately?" → UI reads the local entity table (optimistic), outbox state joined for badges.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first version deleted the outbox row before the network call ("so it won't resend"), reasoning that failures would re-enqueue. A process kill between those two points produced the 3% loss. Reversing the order, and adding the idempotency key, was a two-line fix after three weeks of chasing server logs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: in-memory retry loop.
  • Hire: Room outbox + WorkManager + backoff, observes state with Flow.
  • Strong hire: idempotency, per-entity ordering with bounded parallelism, conflict policy, cancellation/process-death proof ordering of ack vs delete, and metrics.

questions.contextHtml: Chat screen. Messages come from three sources: Room (history, source of truth), a WebSocket (live), and a REST "catch-up since cursor" call run on reconnect. Users report duplicate messages after a flaky-network reconnect (~0.7% of sessions), messages out of order, and the list jumping when the keyboard opens. Average conversation: 5K messages, 60 live messages/min in group chats. Message ids are server-assigned; locally sent messages have a client id until acked.
questions.promptHtml: Design the data flow so the UI is a pure function of the DB, duplicates are impossible, and reconnects are correct. Where do Flow and coroutines go?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: merge(socketFlow, dbFlow) into a MutableList in the ViewModel. This double-counts, loses ordering, and conflates two sources of truth.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a monotonic server sequence/cursor per conversation? Are edits/deletes delivered over the socket? Does the socket guarantee delivery after reconnect (no)? How are local pending messages represented?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add @PrimaryKey on server message id with OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE (or upsert) so duplicates collapse at the DB; sort by (serverSeq, clientCreatedAt).
  3. Hypotheses (for duplicates), ranked: socket and catch-up both deliver the same message; optimistic local message with client id plus acked server copy shown together; two socket collectors after reconnect (old job not cancelled); merge of DB and socket in UI.
  4. How I'd verify: log message ids per source; test with a fake socket replaying overlapping ranges; check collector count via coroutine dump.
  5. Design: single source of truth; the socket and REST are both writers into Room, the UI is only a reader of Room.
// Writers
class ChatSync(private val socket: ChatSocket, private val api: ChatApi, private val dao: MessageDao, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    fun start(convId: String): Job = scope.launch {
        socket.connectionState(convId)                      // Flow<Connected|Disconnected>
            .distinctUntilChanged()
            .collectLatest { st ->                          // new connection cancels old session work
                if (st == Connected) coroutineScope {
                    launch { catchUp(convId) }              // REST since cursor -> dao.upsertAll
                    launch { socket.messages(convId).collect { dao.upsert(it.toEntity()) } }
                }
            }
    }
    private suspend fun catchUp(id: String) {
        val cursor = dao.maxSeq(id) ?: 0
        dao.upsertAll(api.since(id, cursor).map { it.toEntity() })
    }
}
// Reader
@Query("SELECT * FROM message WHERE convId = :id ORDER BY seq, clientTs")
fun observe(id: String): Flow<List<MessageEntity>>   // or PagingSource for long histories

Optimistic send: insert with state=SENDING, clientId; on ack UPDATE ... SET serverId, seq WHERE clientId in a transaction so there is never a visible second row. Dedup identity: (convId, serverId) unique plus clientId unique index. collectLatest on the connection state ensures a reconnect cancels the previous session's launches (structured concurrency); the coroutineScope makes catch-up and live both children so a failure in one cancels the session instead of leaving a half-connected state, and the outer retry/backoff re-establishes it. 6. Fix path: migrate with a DB migration adding unique indexes (dedupe existing rows first with DELETE ... WHERE rowid NOT IN (SELECT MIN(rowid) ... GROUP BY convId, serverId)). 7. Prevention: property-based test: random interleavings of socket/REST/ack events must converge to the same final table; metric: duplicate-insert conflicts count; LeakCanary for socket listeners. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not merge in the UI. Not a SharedFlow buffer as a cache. Not Dispatchers.IO per message insert; batch inserts when bursts arrive (buffer + chunked-style time window with collect batching) to avoid hammering Room with 60 invalidations/min times many chats. UI: use stable key = messageId in LazyColumn/DiffUtil so the list does not jump; keep scroll anchor on the newest item unless the user scrolled up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Catch-up and live arrive interleaved with a gap?" → Gap detection by seq: if incoming.seq > maxSeq + 1, trigger catch-up from maxSeq.
  • "Socket flood: 500 msgs/s in a huge channel?" → Batch in time windows (e.g. 100-250 ms) before upsert; never one transaction per message.
  • "Why collectLatest rather than flatMapLatest?" → Both cancel prior work; here the body is a side-effect session, so collectLatest reads naturally.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" in-memory merge of socket and DB shipped for a deadline. It produced duplicates only on reconnect storms. Making the DB the sole truth deleted 200 lines of merge logic and the whole bug class.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: merges flows in UI.
  • Hire: Room as source of truth, sockets/REST write to it, unique keys.
  • Strong hire: reconnect session handling with structured concurrency, optimistic-send reconciliation, gap detection, batching under load, convergence tests.

questions.subtopic: Download manager with progress and cancellation
questions.contextHtml:
A video app lets users download episodes (200 MB-1.2 GB). Bugs reported: cancelling a download leaves a partial file and a still-running network connection (data usage keeps going); the progress bar jumps and the UI janks (progress emitted ~12K times/second on Wi-Fi); on low-memory devices OOM occurs; two quick taps start two downloads of the same file. Code:

fun download(url: String, dest: File): Flow<Progress> = flow {
    val resp = client.newCall(Request.Builder().url(url).build()).execute()  // blocking
    val body = resp.body!!
    val total = body.contentLength()
    var read = 0L
    val buf = ByteArray(512)
    body.byteStream().use { input ->
        dest.outputStream().use { out ->
            while (true) {
                val n = input.read(buf)
                if (n == -1) break
                out.write(buf, 0, n)
                read += n
                emit(Progress(read, total))
            }
        }
    }
    emit(Progress(total, total))
}

Collected with viewModelScope.launch { download(...).collect { _progress.value = it } }.
questions.promptHtml: List every defect and write the corrected version.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)." Fixes the main-thread network, but not cancellation of blocking I/O, partial files, throttling, resume, or double starts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Resume required (HTTP Range)? Must downloads continue when the app is backgrounded (then WorkManager/foreground service, not a VM scope)? Checksum available? Storage target (app-specific vs scoped storage)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-flag to cap concurrent downloads to 1; patch cancellation first because it leaks data.
  3. Defects, ranked:
    • (a) execute() + blocking read are not cancellable by coroutine cancellation: cancelling the collector only takes effect at the next emit (which checks the job), but a stalled read can block indefinitely and the socket stays open.
    • (b) No cleanup of the partial file on cancel/failure; no atomic rename.
    • (c) 512-byte buffer: 1.2 GB = ~2.4M iterations and 2.4M emits; use 8-64 KB.
    • (d) Emits every read: unbounded UI work; conflate/sample.
    • (e) Runs on the collector's dispatcher (Main if collected from VM): execute() on main would throw NetworkOnMainThreadException; flowOn required.
    • (f) resp is never closed on exceptions before use (body!! NPE risk, and resp is leaked if contentLength throws).
    • (g) No dedupe: two taps = two concurrent writers to the same file.
    • (h) Progress(total, total) with total == -1 (chunked response) is wrong.
  4. How I'd verify: StrictMode, Network Profiler for the still-open connection, lsof-style check via adb shell, a test with MockWebServer using SocketPolicy.NO_RESPONSE/throttled body for stalled reads.
  5. Root cause (cancellation): Coroutine cancellation is cooperative. Flow.emit and ensureActive() are cancellation points; blocking InputStream.read is not. For OkHttp, the bridge is to cancel the Call when the coroutine is cancelled.
  6. Fix:
fun download(url: String, dest: File): Flow<Progress> = callbackFlow {   // or channelFlow
    val tmp = File(dest.parentFile, dest.name + ".part")
    val call = client.newCall(Request.Builder().url(url).build())
    val job = launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
        try {
            call.execute().use { resp ->
                check(resp.isSuccessful) { "HTTP ${resp.code}" }
                val body = checkNotNull(resp.body)
                val total = body.contentLength()                    // may be -1
                var read = 0L
                val buf = ByteArray(32 * 1024)
                body.source().inputStream().use { input ->
                    tmp.outputStream().buffered().use { out ->
                        while (true) {
                            ensureActive()                          // cooperative check each chunk
                            val n = input.read(buf); if (n == -1) break
                            out.write(buf, 0, n); read += n
                            trySend(Progress(read, total))          // conflated by buffer policy below
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            check(tmp.renameTo(dest)) { "rename failed" }
            close()
        } catch (e: Throwable) {
            tmp.delete()
            close(e)
        }
    }
    awaitClose { call.cancel(); job.cancel(); }                     // kills the socket read -> IOException
}.buffer(Channel.CONFLATED)                                          // keep only the latest progress
 .sample(200)                                                        // UI cadence; @FlowPreview-era API, check version

sample is @FlowPreview through the 1.x line; if I want zero preview APIs I compute the percent and only trySend when it changes by >= 1% or 200 ms elapsed. call.cancel() makes the blocked read throw IOException("Canceled"), which is what actually frees the connection. Failure branch deletes the .part file; success does an atomic renameTo. For resume, keep .part, send Range: bytes=<size>-, and validate with ETag/If-Range. Single-flight: keep ConcurrentHashMap<String, StateFlow<DownloadState>> or a Mutex-guarded map in a singleton DownloadManager scoped to an app-level CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) (not GlobalScope); a second request for the same key returns the existing flow. 7. Prevention: MockWebServer cancellation test (assert server-side connection closed within N ms), file-state assertions after cancel/failure, benchmark UI frame time during download, WorkManager (long-running, foreground notification) when downloads must outlive the screen. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not withContext(Dispatchers.IO) with runInterruptible as the only mechanism: runInterruptible does help for interruptible blocking calls, but OkHttp/Okio sockets do not reliably respond to thread interrupt; Call.cancel() is the correct hook. Not Channel.UNLIMITED for progress. Not VM scope if the download must survive navigation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Pause/resume?" → Pause = cancel the call but keep .part; resume uses Range; persist offset.
  • "Parallel chunked download?" → Semaphore-limited ranges written with RandomAccessFile/FileChannel at offsets; more complexity, only worth it for very large files on fast links.
  • "Disk full?" → IOException caught, .part deleted, surface a typed StorageFull error; check usableSpace up front.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: "Cancel" in a release looked fine in the UI, but users reported data caps burned. The cause was exactly the uncancelled blocking read: the collector stopped, the socket kept pulling bytes until the server finished.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only flowOn(IO).
  • Hire: finds cancellation, buffer size, throttling, partial file cleanup.
  • Strong hire: Call.cancel() in awaitClose, atomic rename, resume with Range, single-flight dedupe, process-lifetime scope choice, and a cancellation test.

questions.contextHtml:
You bumped Kotlin 1.9 -> 2.0 and kotlinx.coroutines 1.6.4 -> 1.8.x in one PR (also AGP and a few libs). Staged rollout at 10% of 2M DAU. Crashlytics 40 minutes later: new crash cluster, 1.9% of sessions, device-agnostic, OS 8-14:

Fatal Exception: java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: No static method
  <someMethod>(Lkotlinx/coroutines/flow/Flow;...)... in class Lkotlinx/coroutines/flow/FlowKt;
    at com.vendor.analytics.EventPipeline$start$1.invokeSuspend(Unknown Source)
    at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resume(ContinuationImpl.kt)

Also a second, smaller cluster: IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize on 0.1% of sessions (mostly one OEM). Your own code compiles and unit tests pass.
questions.promptHtml: Triage this. How do you stop the rollout safely, find the cause, and make upgrades like this safe in future?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert the upgrade." Fine as step one but no explanation: does not distinguish binary vs source compatibility, never inspects the resolved dependency graph, and treats both clusters as one cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which library owns the failing frame (a vendor SDK, "Unknown Source" = no line numbers, so likely minified/third-party)? Did the vendor SDK ship with its own copy or depend on coroutines transitively? Is R8 full mode enabled (default since AGP 8.0)? Is the Main dispatcher cluster OEM-specific or R8-related? Which other libs moved in the PR?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout (Play Console "halt"), roll back to the previous release for the 10% via a hotfix of the previous binary, keep the crash cluster IDs as the regression test target. Do not "forward fix" under pressure with 4 simultaneous changes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) binary incompatibility: the vendor SDK was compiled against an older coroutines/Flow API that no longer exists with the same JVM signature in 1.8 (compiled inline/@PublishedApi/hidden-deprecated members are the usual victims); (b) Kotlin 2.0 (K2) compiled inline functions or default-arg synthetic bridges differently, breaking an SDK that is itself compiled with the old compiler against your new stdlib/coroutines; (c) duplicate classes via a fat-jar SDK that bundles a private copy of coroutines; (d) R8 stripped the ServiceLoader entry for MainDispatcherFactory (second cluster).
  4. How I'd verify: ./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --dependency kotlinx-coroutines-core --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath to see who forced which version; ./gradlew :app:dependencies; inspect the SDK AAR/jar with javap to see which FlowKt method it calls; check the library's changelog for its supported coroutines range; retrace the crash with the release mapping.txt; for Main dispatcher, check R8's configuration.txt/usage.txt and consumer rules, test with isMinifyEnabled=true on a release-like build on the OEM device; reproduce via instrumented smoke test of the vendor SDK entry point.
  5. Root cause (what I'd state, with honesty): Gradle resolves one version per module: the highest requested wins. That silently upgraded the version the SDK ran against, and the SDK was compiled against a signature that is not present in the new artifact. Source-compat tests can't see this; only runtime exercise does. I would confirm the exact API from javap rather than assert which one it is; I am not going to guess a specific removed method. The Main-dispatcher cluster is a separate cause family (init failure/R8/ServiceLoader) and must be treated as a separate ticket.
  6. Fix: Short term: pin kotlinx-coroutines-bom to a version both we and the SDK support, or upgrade the vendor SDK to a release built for it; if the vendor is slow, isolate behind our interface so we can swap them. Long term: upgrade in separate PRs: Kotlin first, then coroutines, then AGP; each shipped through staged rollout with its own diff.
// build.gradle.kts: pin deliberately and document why
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-bom:1.8.1"))
    constraints {
        implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core") { because("vendor SDK X 4.2 verified; see PR #…") }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Run a smoke/instrumented test suite against a minified release-like variant in CI (testBuildType), including every third-party SDK entry point; Renovate/Dependabot groups with one library family per PR; keep a "dependency compat matrix"; Android vitals/Crashlytics alert on new fatal signature in staged rollout (auto-halt at > 0.2% sessions); dependency lock files (--write-locks) so transitive bumps show up in review.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not exclude group: kotlinx.coroutines on the SDK (would force the same mismatch). Not downgrading just coroutines while keeping Kotlin 2 without checking compatibility (the Kotlin and coroutines versions are loosely coupled but it must be validated). Not shipping a try/catch for NoSuchMethodError (an Error, masks a broken integration).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Vendor says they don't support the new version for 3 months." → Wrap the SDK behind our own interface, keep old coroutines only if it is the sole consumer (can't have two versions in one app without shading/relocation), or ship the new Kotlin/coroutines later behind the vendor's fix; evaluate replacing the vendor.
  • "How could unit tests pass?" → Unit tests don't run the vendor SDK minified on-device; JVM tests may stub it.
  • "Do I need to match Kotlin and coroutines versions?" → Not exactly, but each coroutines release is built against a specific Kotlin version and the Kotlin compiler warns on pre-release metadata; read the release notes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "routine" bump touched five libs in one PR; the crash signature pointed at a vendor SDK nobody had touched in a year. The team lost a day bisecting before someone ran dependencyInsight and found a transitive version forced two majors up through a BOM.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: revert only, or blames Kotlin generically.
  • Hire: halts rollout, uses dependencyInsight, separates the two clusters.
  • Strong hire: explains binary vs source compat and Gradle conflict resolution, verifies with javap/retrace instead of guessing, proposes minified-variant CI tests, auto-halt thresholds, and one-library-per-PR policy.

questions.contextHtml:
Photo-editing app, OOM crash rate 0.9% (up from 0.2%) on 2-3 GB devices after adding a "background export" feature. LeakCanary (debug) reports:

┬───
│ GC Root: Thread (kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor)
├─ kotlinx.coroutines.StandaloneCoroutine
│    Leaking: UNKNOWN
├─ com.app.export.ExportManager$export$1
│    ↓ ExportManager$export$1.$onDone (captured lambda)
├─ com.app.editor.EditorFragment$$ExternalSyntheticLambda3
│    ↓ EditorFragment.binding
╰→ android.widget.FrameLayout  Leaking: YES (View detached)

Code:

object ExportManager {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default)
    fun export(project: Project, onDone: (File) -> Unit) {
        scope.launch {
            val file = render(project)          // 30-90 s, 120 MB bitmap working set
            withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { onDone(file) }
        }
    }
}
// Fragment
ExportManager.export(project) { file -> binding.progress.isVisible = false; share(file) }
questions.promptHtml: Explain the leak, and fix it without breaking "export continues when user leaves the screen".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use viewModelScope." That cancels export when the user leaves, violating the requirement, and ignores that the callback captured the fragment.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must export survive process death (then WorkManager/foreground service)? Multiple concurrent exports? Where should the result be delivered if the screen is gone?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a weak/nulling pattern: not ideal, but a quick patch is to stop passing view-capturing lambdas into the singleton. Ship a cap on concurrent exports (Semaphore(1)) to bound memory.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lambda -> Fragment -> view binding retained by long-lived singleton scope; (b) the scope is never cancelled and holds render bitmaps while queued; (c) unbounded concurrent exports; (d) Bitmap not recycled/reused (red herring: bitmaps are GC-managed on API 26+, pixel data lives on native heap and is freed with the object).
  4. How I'd verify: the LeakCanary trace above (GC root -> coroutine -> lambda -> Fragment). Heap dump in Android Studio; Memory Profiler allocation tracking on repeated export/exit; adb shell dumpsys meminfo.
  5. Root cause: A coroutine is a heap object graph: its continuation holds every captured variable until the coroutine completes. ExportManager is a process-lifetime singleton with a scope that is never cancelled, so any running coroutine is a GC root path to everything captured. The captured onDone lambda holds the fragment (and its binding). Note: Dispatchers.Main hop is fine; the leak is the captured reference, not the dispatcher.
  6. Fix: Decouple the work (process-scoped) from the UI (lifecycle-scoped). Expose results as state, not callbacks:
class ExportManager(private val appScope: CoroutineScope /* SupervisorJob() + Default, provided by DI */) {
    private val permits = Semaphore(1)
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<Map<String, ExportState>>(emptyMap())
    val state: StateFlow<Map<String, ExportState>> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun export(project: Project) {
        appScope.launch {
            permits.withPermit {
                _state.update { it + (project.id to ExportState.Running) }
                val result = runCatching { render(project) }
                    .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
                _state.update { it + (project.id to result.toState()) }
            }
        }
    }
}
// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        manager.state.map { it[project.id] }.distinctUntilChanged().collect(::render)
    }
}

The singleton now holds only data (no view references). If the user leaves, export continues; when they return they re-subscribe and see the current state. For "must survive process death or be reliable under Doze", the heavy work belongs in a CoroutineWorker with a foreground-service notification; appScope is fine for in-process continuation only. 7. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug; a code-review rule "no callbacks/lambdas from UI into singletons; expose Flow/StateFlow"; instrumentation test that rotates/exit-enters 20 times and asserts heap object count for EditorFragment; inject scopes so tests can cancel them. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not GlobalScope (no owner, no cancellation, no test control). Not WeakReference<Fragment> callbacks: it hides the leak but result delivery becomes nondeterministic. Not SupervisorJob omission: a plain Job in the app scope would cancel all exports when one fails.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why SupervisorJob for the app scope?" → One failing child must not cancel siblings or the scope itself; with a plain Job, the first failure cancels everything and the scope is dead for later launches.
  • "Should the process scope be cancelled ever?" → It lives and dies with the process; cancel it only in tests.
  • "Where do uncaught exceptions go?" → Add a CoroutineExceptionHandler to the scope for launch roots that logs to Crashlytics (non-fatal) so a bug doesn't crash the app unintentionally, but decide it deliberately.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 'quick' singleton scope was copied from a blog post as an easy way to survive rotation. Six months later it had 14 call sites, each capturing a different screen. The fix was an afternoon; finding them was two sprints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "memory leak, use viewModelScope".
  • Hire: explains capture chain, moves to state-exposing singleton with lifecycle-aware collection.
  • Strong hire: SupervisorJob rationale, concurrency bound, process-death story (WorkManager), tests for leak regressions.

questions.contextHtml:
You are reviewing a PR from a mid-level dev. The screen shows a list of orders with pull-to-refresh. QA reports: the spinner sometimes never stops, a crash IllegalStateException: Cannot invoke setValue on a background thread, errors toast "randomly" missing, and memory climbs after repeated navigation. Code:

class OrdersViewModel(
    private val repo: OrdersRepo,
    private val context: Context,                 // injected from Activity
) : ViewModel() {

    val orders = MutableLiveData<List<Order>>()
    val loading = MutableStateFlow(false)
    val events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>()

    init {
        GlobalScope.launch {
            repo.observeOrders().collect { orders.postValue(it) }
        }
    }

    fun refresh() {
        viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            try {
                loading.value = true
                orders.value = repo.fetchOrders()
                loading.value = false
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                events.emit(UiEvent.ShowError(e.message ?: context.getString(R.string.generic_error)))
            }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find at least six defects, rank them by production impact, and show the corrected class.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots "GlobalScope" and "exposes mutable" only. Misses the CancellationException swallow and the lost one-shot events.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is events meant to be one-shot (navigation/toast)? Is observeOrders() a Room Flow? Does Context need to be Activity or app?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The crash (setValue off main) and stuck spinner are the user-visible ones; hotfix finally { loading.value = false } and postValue/withContext(Main) ordering, then clean refactor.
  3. Defects, ranked by impact:
    1. orders.value = ... inside Dispatchers.IO: LiveData.setValue must be on main -> the reported crash. (StateFlow value is thread-safe; LiveData's is not.)
    2. Spinner never stops: loading.value = false is skipped on exception; no finally. Also on cancellation.
    3. catch (e: Exception) swallows CancellationException: on VM clear the catch runs events.emit(...) inside a cancelled coroutine (it throws again at the suspension point, but the intent is wrong) and breaks the structured-cancellation contract; always rethrow it.
    4. GlobalScope.launch in init: never cancelled; keeps collecting after onCleared, holds orders (and thus the VM, and UI observers via LiveData) -> the memory growth, multiplied per navigation.
    5. Context in ViewModel (an Activity context): leaks the Activity across config changes; if a string is needed, inject Application or a StringProvider/pass a @StringRes to the UI.
    6. MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>() with no replay/buffer and no subscriber: events emitted while the UI is stopped (rotation, background) are dropped, i.e. the "missing toast". Plus exposing MutableSharedFlow, MutableLiveData, MutableStateFlow publicly lets any caller write.
    7. Bonus: mixing LiveData and Flow in one VM; two sources for UI truth.
  4. How I'd verify: reproduce the crash with StrictMode/a unit test using Dispatchers.setMain; LeakCanary for the Activity; collect events from a stopped lifecycle in a test.
  5. Root cause: a mix of thread-confinement mistakes (LiveData), lifecycle/ownership mistakes (GlobalScope, Context), and coroutine contract mistakes (swallowed cancellation, no finally).
  6. Fix:
class OrdersViewModel(private val repo: OrdersRepo) : ViewModel() {

    private val _loading = MutableStateFlow(false)
    private val _events = Channel<UiEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)        // buffered: not lost while UI stopped
    val events: Flow<UiEvent> = _events.receiveAsFlow()              // single consumer, each event once

    val orders: StateFlow<List<Order>> = repo.observeOrders()
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
    val loading: StateFlow<Boolean> = _loading.asStateFlow()

    fun refresh() {
        if (_loading.value) return
        viewModelScope.launch {                                      // Main by default; repo is main-safe
            _loading.value = true
            try {
                repo.refresh()                                       // writes to Room; orders updates via Flow
            } catch (e: CancellationException) {
                throw e
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                _events.send(UiEvent.ShowError(e.message))           // UI maps null to a string resource
            } finally {
                _loading.value = false
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: PR checklist (GlobalScope banned by detekt GlobalCoroutineUsage; Context in VM flagged; mutable types never public; every catch (Exception) in suspend code rethrows cancellation); a VM unit-test template with MainDispatcherRule.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Channel vs SharedFlow(replay=0): a Channel buffers while no collector exists but delivers to one collector only; if two UI consumers needed it, use state-based events ("consumed" flag in StateFlow). I would not use SharedFlow(replay=1) for events: it re-delivers on rotation. Also I'd not add Dispatchers.IO in the VM; the repository owns its dispatcher (main-safety).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not postValue?" → It's thread-safe but coalesces rapid updates (only the last is delivered) and delays; wrong for event-like data.
  • "Is a Channel event still lost on process death/backgrounded collector?" → Buffered survives rotation (VM survives), not process death; if the event must persist, put it in state.
  • "finally with a suspend call?" → Wrap in withContext(NonCancellable) if the cleanup suspends and the coroutine may be cancelled.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "random missing toast" was open for a month; the cause was SharedFlow events emitted during a configuration change. The team replaced all event flows with a tiny Channel-based helper and the ticket class disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds 1-2 style issues.
  • Hire: finds 5-6 correct defects including setValue-thread, finally, GlobalScope, Context.
  • Strong hire: also finds cancellation swallow and event loss, explains Channel-vs-SharedFlow trade-off, and proposes tooling (detekt, tests) to prevent recurrence.

questions.contextHtml:
Ride-sharing app, 1.2M DAU. Android vitals flags "excessive background GPS" and battery team measures +4.8% battery/hour for users who open the app then switch away (the app is not in a trip). Perfetto/Battery Historian show the fused location provider requesting updates every 1 s for the entire session, including while backgrounded. Code:

class LocationRepository(@AppScope scope: CoroutineScope, client: FusedLocationProviderClient) {
    val location: SharedFlow<Location> = callbackFlow {
        val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
            override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) { r.lastLocation?.let(::trySend) }
        }
        client.requestLocationUpdates(
            LocationRequest.Builder(Priority.PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY, 1_000).build(), cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
    }.shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 1)
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the problems, quantify the impact, and fix without breaking the "driver nearby" map when the user returns within a few seconds.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WhileSubscribed." Right keyword but misses the missing awaitClose (so even with WhileSubscribed, updates never stop), and misses collector-side lifecycle (a collector in lifecycleScope.launch keeps the subscription while stopped).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens truly need 1 s updates? Is background location a product requirement outside trips? What accuracy is needed in browse mode (city-level vs 10 m)? Foreground service during active trips?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-config to raise the interval to 10 s and priority to PRIORITY_BALANCED_POWER_ACCURACY in browse mode; this alone cuts GPS duty cycle. Then ship the lifecycle fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Eagerly starts at construction and never stops (the upstream is tied to scope, the app process); (b) no awaitClose { removeLocationUpdates }: callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException if its block returns without suspending in awaitClose, so the snippet as pasted would fail right after registering (a simplified paste of the real code, probably); in any variant, nothing ever unregisters the callback, so even a correct WhileSubscribed could not stop the GPS. I'd flag it either way; (c) UI collectors use lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect } which keeps collecting in the background; (d) high-accuracy priority + 1 s interval is overkill outside trips.
  4. How I'd verify: Battery Historian + adb shell dumpsys location (active requests per package), Perfetto power and location tracks, Android Studio Energy Profiler (location requests), breakpoint/log in removeLocationUpdates.
  5. Root cause: A hot flow's lifetime is decided by SharingStarted, not by the UI. Eagerly ties the upstream (and the OS registration) to the process lifetime; without a cleanup in awaitClose, cancellation of the upstream can't release the OS resource.
  6. Fix:
class LocationRepository(@AppScope scope: CoroutineScope, private val client: FusedLocationProviderClient) {

    private fun updates(intervalMs: Long, priority: Int): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
        val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
            override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) { r.lastLocation?.let { trySend(it) } }
        }
        val req = LocationRequest.Builder(priority, intervalMs).build()
        client.requestLocationUpdates(req, cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
        awaitClose { client.removeLocationUpdates(cb) }              // releases GPS on cancellation
    }.conflate()                                                     // slow consumer sees latest fix only

    val location: SharedFlow<Location> = updates(2_000, Priority.PRIORITY_BALANCED_POWER_ACCURACY)
        .shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 30_000), replay = 1)
}
// UI
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { repo.location.collect(::render) }
}

WhileSubscribed(5_000) keeps the upstream alive across rotation (< 5 s gap) and stops it when the last collector goes away; replayExpirationMillis stops serving a stale fix after 30 s so the map does not show a driver positions based on 2-minute-old location. Collector-side repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) (lifecycle-runtime-ktx 2.4+) ensures the collector leaves when the app goes to background, which triggers the stop timeout. In Compose use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() (lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.6+). Trip mode: a separate foreground-service path with PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY, explicitly started and stopped by trip state. 7. Prevention: a test with a fake client asserting removeLocationUpdates is called ~5 s after the last collector cancels (virtual time with runTest, advanceTimeBy(5_001)); vitals alert; review rule: every callbackFlow ends with awaitClose { unregister }; every hot flow uses WhileSubscribed unless it is a documented process-lifetime stream. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: stopTimeout = 0 saves battery but restarts GPS on every rotation (cold start can take seconds to first fix); Lazily/Eagerly only when the upstream is cheap and always needed. I'd not poll lastLocation in a loop as a replacement; it is cheap but can be stale/null. Remember the background-location permission/policy implications (API 29+ ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Show the last known driver positions instantly on return?" → Keep replay = 1 plus a persisted last-known Location for the first frame, marked stale in UI.
  • "Compose recomposition on every fix?" → distinctUntilChanged by rounded coordinates, conflate, and derive map camera updates in snapshotFlow.
  • "Two features need different intervals?" → Don't share one flow; share a base stream at the finest required interval and downsample per consumer with sample() / debounce(), or reference-count requests in a repo.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The bug stayed hidden for months because dev devices were always plugged in. It was found when a battery dashboard split cohorts by "time in background after open". Fixing the awaitClose and WhileSubscribed recovered about half of the regression; lowering priority outside trips recovered the rest.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the OS or lowers interval only.
  • Hire: WhileSubscribed + awaitClose + lifecycle-aware collection.
  • Strong hire: explains replay expiration, rotation-vs-background timeout trade-off, separate trip mode, testing with virtual time, and policy limits.

questions.contextHtml: App with 380K lines, 70% of data layer in RxJava 2/3 (Single, Observable, BehaviorSubject, PublishSubject, flatMap, combineLatest), ~40 engineers, 3.2M DAU, crash-free rate 99.7% that leadership will not let you drop. Mandate: move to coroutines/Flow over 12 months without a rewrite freeze. Known pain: RxJava UndeliverableException crashes (0.15% of sessions), thread-hopping bugs, test flakiness.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the migration plan: ordering, interop mechanics, behavior differences that will bite you, and how you de-risk each step in production.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Convert file by file with the IDE." Ignores semantic differences (errors, hot/cold, backpressure, threading), interop boundaries, and rollout safety.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Rx2 or Rx3? Which layers expose Rx (UI, domain, data)? How is DI done? Who owns shared modules? Any Rx-only operators in use (window, buffer, custom transformers)? Test coverage of the riskiest flows?
  2. Immediate mitigation (stop the bleeding): Install RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler { } (log + report non-fatal) to neutralize UndeliverableException crashes before touching architecture, since those exist today. Freeze new Rx code via lint/detekt rule.
  3. Hypotheses (about what will go wrong): (a) error semantics differ; (b) threading changes (subscribeOn/observeOn vs dispatchers/flowOn); (c) hot sources (Subject) behave differently as SharedFlow/StateFlow (replay, conflation, equality); (d) disposal vs cancellation; (e) backpressure.
  4. How I'd verify: Characterization tests before each conversion; shadow-run (old and new path both execute, compare outputs, ship only the old result) for risky pipelines; Crashlytics non-fatals by migration tag; staged rollout by feature flag.
  5. Plan: Strangler by seams, bottom-up for logic and top-down for entry points:
Phase 0  guardrails: Rx error handler, lint "no new Rx", testing utilities (Turbine, runTest)
Phase 1  interop module (kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 / -rx2): asFlow(), asObservable(), await(), rxSingle{}, rxObservable{}
Phase 2  new code in Flow/suspend, exposed at the edge as Rx via adapters where old callers remain
Phase 3  convert leaf data sources (Retrofit: Single -> suspend; Room: Rx DAOs -> suspend/Flow)
Phase 4  convert repositories (Subject caches -> StateFlow/SharedFlow)
Phase 5  ViewModels/UI collectors to repeatOnLifecycle / collectAsStateWithLifecycle
Phase 6  remove adapters, remove Rx dependencies, remove error handler

Mapping to remember: Single -> suspend fun; cold Observable -> Flow; BehaviorSubject -> MutableStateFlow (distinct by equals, conflated, requires initial value) or MutableSharedFlow(replay=1) if equal values must re-emit; PublishSubject -> MutableSharedFlow(); flatMap -> flatMapMerge; switchMap -> flatMapLatest; concatMap -> flatMapConcat; combineLatest -> combine; observeOn -> flowOn affects upstream only (opposite direction from observeOn), so in Flow you collect on the collector's context; subscribeOn ~ flowOn upstream; Disposable.dispose() ~ Job.cancel(), and CompositeDisposable ~ structured scope. Behavioral traps: (1) Rx treats an error as a terminal signal delivered to onError; coroutines propagate exceptions up the Job hierarchy and can crash through launch if unhandled. (2) StateFlow drops equal consecutive values; BehaviorSubject emits them. (3) Rx Single errors thrown after disposal go to the global handler; coroutines silently cancel. (4) rxSingle { } runs on Dispatchers.Default unless you pass a context; no automatic main thread. 6. Fix path example (leaf):

// before
fun user(id: String): Single<User> = api.user(id).subscribeOn(Schedulers.io())
// after: new truth, old callers served by adapter
suspend fun user(id: String): User = api.user(id)                         // Retrofit suspend, main-safe
fun userRx(id: String): Single<User> = rxSingle(Dispatchers.IO) { user(id) }   // deprecated bridge
  1. Prevention: a migration dashboard (count of Rx imports per module; fail CI if increasing); per-module owners; "done" definition = no Rx imports + tests on runTest; release train cadence: at most one risky layer per release.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang rewrite, no "convert everything under a flag day". Not wrapping every Rx chain in asFlow() forever: adapters are scaffolding with an expiry date. Keep Rx where it genuinely fits (complex time-window operators; library APIs that expose Rx) unless the team can pay for rewriting it. Consider that Rx 3's Maybe/Completable map to nullable return / Unit suspend.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "How do you prove no behavior change in a pipeline with debounce and retryWhen?" → Marble-style tests on both versions with virtual time (TestScheduler for Rx, runTest + advanceTimeBy for Flow); same event script, compare outputs.
  • "A Subject is used as an event bus across modules." → Replace with a typed SharedFlow behind an interface; decide replay/buffer explicitly (extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow); this is where hidden coupling surfaces.
  • "Thread-safety of mutable shared state previously guarded by observeOn(single)?" → Serialize with a Mutex, a single-threaded dispatcher via limitedParallelism(1), or confine in an actor-style Channel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The migration looked 60% complete by file count and was 20% by risk: the hardest 15% were Subject-based caches with undocumented replay semantics. We converted them last, with shadow comparisons, and the number of production incidents attributed to the migration was two minor, both from StateFlow equality dropping an intentionally repeated value.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: file-by-file conversion with no safety plan.
  • Hire: interop adapters, bottom-up order, operator mapping, flags.
  • Strong hire: calls out error/threading/hot-flow semantic differences, global error handler first, shadow runs and characterization tests, lint-based freeze, explicit end date for adapters.

questions.subtopic: Polling repository with backoff and lifecycle
questions.contextHtml: Order-tracking screen must show status updates; the backend has no push channel yet (push is 2 quarters away). 600K concurrent users at peak; backend capacity is 40K req/s for this endpoint, current clients poll every 2 s with a while(true) in lifecycleScope, which at peak is 300K req/s equivalent if everyone is on-screen, and during a partial outage retries are immediate, producing a retry storm. Requirements: fresh within ~5 s while visible, minimal load, graceful under failures, nothing running in background, stop when status is terminal (DELIVERED/CANCELLED).
questions.promptHtml: Design the polling repository, including backoff, jitter, lifecycle, and testability.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: while (true) { fetch(); delay(2000) } with a bare try/catch that continues. No backoff, no jitter, swallows cancellation, polls in background, and cannot be tested without waiting real time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the server return ETag/304, or a suggested Retry-After/pollAfterMs? Is ordering guaranteed? What's the terminal state set? Can the server shed load by returning 429/503 with headers? Is a 5 s staleness hard or soft?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-config: raise the base interval to 5 s now (a 2.5x reduction: 600K / 2 s = 300K rps vs 600K / 5 s = 120K rps, still above the 40K capacity, so tell the backend this still needs caching/CDN or a coalescing layer, not just client changes), add jitter, stop on terminal state. Honest math: clients alone cannot fix a 3x capacity gap; pair with server-side caching of the status.
  3. Hypotheses (for the retry storm), ranked: immediate retry on error; synchronized clients after an outage (thundering herd); polling continues in background; polling terminal orders.
  4. How I'd verify: server request-rate graph per client version; simulate with a load script of 10K fake clients; unit-test the schedule with virtual time.
  5. Design: the repository exposes a cold Flow<OrderStatus>; the schedule lives inside the flow so cancellation stops everything.
fun observeStatus(id: String): Flow<OrderStatus> = flow {
    var failures = 0
    while (true) {
        val result = runCatching { api.status(id) }
        result.exceptionOrNull()?.let { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
        val wait: Long = result.fold(
            onSuccess = { s ->
                failures = 0
                emit(s)
                if (s.isTerminal) return@flow                         // completes the flow: no more polling
                (s.pollAfterMs ?: 5_000L)                             // server can steer cadence
            },
            onFailure = { e ->
                failures++
                backoffMs(failures, e)
            },
        )
        delay(wait + Random.nextLong(0, wait / 5))                    // up to +20% jitter
    }
}.distinctUntilChanged()

private fun backoffMs(attempt: Int, e: Throwable): Long {
    val retryAfter = (e as? HttpException)?.response()?.headers()?.get("Retry-After")?.toLongOrNull()?.times(1000)
    val exp = (5_000L shl (attempt - 1).coerceAtMost(5)).coerceAtMost(60_000L)   // 5s,10s,20s,40s,60s cap
    return maxOf(exp, retryAfter ?: 0L)
}

Lifecycle: in the ViewModel repo.observeStatus(id).stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Loading), collected via repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED); backgrounded > 5 s -> polling stops, return -> fresh fetch immediately because the cold flow restarts. Show last known value from stateIn (it keeps the last value) while refreshing. Errors are surfaced as a degraded "last updated Xs ago / retrying" UI state emitted from the flow (emit(Stale(...))) so the UI does not freeze silently; an auth error (401/403) or 404 stops the loop with a terminal error instead of backing off forever. 6. Fix path: ship behind a remote config; server later replaces the loop with push/SSE and the repository interface (Flow<OrderStatus>) stays unchanged, which is the real benefit of modelling it as a Flow. 7. Prevention: runTest test: failures produce delays 5/10/20/40/60/60 s (± jitter bounded), success resets, terminal completes the flow, Retry-After is honored; inject Random and Clock/delay policy for determinism. Alert on client request rate per user > threshold. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not WorkManager periodic (15 min minimum, wrong tool for foreground freshness). Not Timer/Handler loops (no structured cancellation). Not long-polling/WebSocket now unless the backend can support it; mention as the next step. Full-jitter vs equal-jitter: full jitter spreads load better for herd problems; I used bounded jitter to keep the freshness guarantee.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Multiple screens poll the same order." → Share via a repository-level shareIn(WhileSubscribed) keyed by order id so one poller serves all collectors.
