  • "Offline (airplane mode)?" → Observe connectivity (ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback as a callbackFlow) and pause the loop instead of burning backoff time; resume on onAvailable.
  • "Battery saver / Doze?" → Foreground-only polling is naturally safe; do not try to poll in Doze.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A partial outage turned into a full one because 500K clients all retried with a fixed 2 s delay and no jitter; recovery took longer than the original fault. A 60-line backoff change plus a server Retry-After header cut the reconnect storm peak by about 70% in the next incident drill.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: while(true) + delay.
  • Hire: exponential backoff, jitter, lifecycle-aware collection, stop on terminal.
  • Strong hire: honest capacity math, server-steered cadence, Retry-After, cancellation-safe error handling, shared poller, virtual-time tests, path to push.

questions.subtopic: Race between DB write and UI read
questions.contextHtml:
Shopping-list app. User taps a checkbox; ~1.1% of taps visually revert (checkbox flickers back, then sometimes corrects after a second). More frequent on slower devices and when the user taps multiple items quickly. Stack: Room (Flow<List<Item>> query), Compose list. Code:

// DAO
@Query("SELECT * FROM item ORDER BY position") fun observe(): Flow<List<Item>>
@Query("SELECT * FROM item WHERE id = :id") suspend fun get(id: Long): Item
@Update suspend fun update(item: Item)

// Repository
suspend fun toggle(id: Long) {
    val item = dao.get(id)
    dao.update(item.copy(checked = !item.checked))
}

// ViewModel
fun onToggle(id: Long) {
    viewModelScope.launch { repo.toggle(id) }
}
// UI state
val items = repo.observe().stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

Additionally a background sync (WorkManager) writes the whole list from the server every 60 s with dao.replaceAll(list).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the race(s) and fix them. What guarantees does Room's Flow give you, and what does it not?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it @Synchronized" or "use postValue". Doesn't see that read-modify-write across two DAO calls is non-atomic, or that sync can overwrite local edits.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who wins on conflict, local or server? Do items have versions/updatedAt? Is replaceAll a delete+insert (then Flow emits an intermediate empty list)? Single-process app?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace the toggle with a single SQL statement (UPDATE item SET checked = NOT checked WHERE id = :id) so there is no read-modify-write gap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Lost update: two rapid taps on the same item both get the same state, both write the same negated value -> second tap has no effect; or a tap and the 60 s sync interleave.
    • (b) Sync overwrites local: replaceAll writes server state that predates the tap -> checkbox reverts until the next sync.
    • (c) replaceAll not transactional: delete then insert emits a transient empty/partial list through the Flow (Room invalidation emits per transaction; if not wrapped in @Transaction, two emissions).
    • (d) UI reads stale item captured in the composable for the toggle (red herring unless it passes !item.checked itself).
  4. How I'd verify: an in-memory Room test running 100 concurrent toggle() calls on the same id and asserting the parity; log every Flow emission with timestamps and a transaction id; Room query logging (setQueryCallback) in debug.
  5. Root cause: Room serializes transactions, but two separate suspend DAO calls are two transactions; nothing prevents interleaving between get and update. Flow emits after a write transaction commits and invalidates the table: it guarantees eventual consistency with the DB, not read-your-writes ordering relative to your own pending coroutines, and not atomicity across operations you didn't group.
  6. Fix:
// 1. atomic toggle in SQL
@Query("UPDATE item SET checked = NOT checked, updatedAt = :now WHERE id = :id")
suspend fun toggle(id: Long, now: Long)

// 2. sync respects local pending edits, in ONE transaction
@Transaction
suspend fun applyServerList(server: List<Item>) {
    val localDirty = dirtyIds()                       // SELECT id FROM item WHERE dirty = 1
    upsertAll(server.filter { it.id !in localDirty })
    deleteMissing(server.map { it.id }, except = localDirty)
}

Mark edits dirty = 1 (and enqueue push via the outbox pattern); the sync pull merges around dirty rows and the push clears dirty after ack, comparing updatedAt/version to avoid clearing a newer local edit. For optimistic UI that must never flicker, layer a small in-memory overlay MutableStateFlow<Map<Long, Boolean>> combined with the DB Flow: combine(dbFlow, overlay) { ... } and clear the overlay once the DB emits matching state. Concurrency of repeated taps: serialize per item with a Mutex keyed map, or rely on the atomic SQL (preferred; no app-level lock). 7. Prevention: concurrency test (runTest + List(100) { async { dao.toggle(1, now) } }.awaitAll()); rule: no read-modify-write across DAO calls without @Transaction or a single SQL statement; @Transaction on every multi-statement DAO method; version columns for server sync. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a global Mutex in the repository (hides the bug class, serializes unrelated writes, doesn't help across WorkManager process boundaries). Not Dispatchers.Main.immediate hacks. Not skipping the overlay if tap latency (DB write + invalidation ~10-50 ms on slow devices) is noticeable; for local DB it usually isn't, so I'd ship the SQL fix and measure first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does Room's Flow sometimes emit the same list twice?" → Invalidation is table-level, not row-level; any write to item re-runs the query. Use distinctUntilChanged() to filter identical results.
  • "Does @Transaction on a suspend DAO method hold a DB connection across suspensions?" → It runs the body in a transaction on Room's transaction executor; keep suspending calls (network) out of it, which would stall other writers.
  • "Two processes (widget + app)?" → Enable multi-instance invalidation (enableMultiInstanceInvalidation()) and still rely on SQL atomicity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team added a repo-wide Mutex and the revert rate dropped but wasn't zero; the remaining case was the background sync in another process. The permanent fix was making the sync dirty-aware, and the final test was a hundred lines of concurrent-toggle assertions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: threads/@Synchronized hand-waving.
  • Hire: identifies non-atomic read-modify-write and sync overwrite; atomic SQL + @Transaction.
  • Strong hire: explains Room invalidation semantics (table-level, post-commit), dirty-flag sync merge, optimistic overlay trade-off, and a concurrent test.

questions.contextHtml: Marketplace app, catalog of 2M listings, 700K DAU. The browse screen has: free-text search, category chips, price range slider, sort order, and "in stock only" toggle. Today each filter change calls loadFirstPage() manually; users report (a) the list jumps back to the top when the screen rotates, (b) results from an old filter appear after a new filter is applied (about 1 in 300 filter changes), (c) the slider fires ~40 requests per drag. Server pages are 30 items; target p95 first-page latency 600 ms. Paging 3 is available (androidx.paging 3.x).
questions.promptHtml: Design the filter-to-list pipeline using Paging 3, Flow and coroutines. What combines with what, where does caching happen, and what survives rotation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Mutates filters in a MutableLiveData, calls repo.load() in each setter, and keeps a MutableList. Cannot explain cachedIn, why flatMapLatest is needed, or what happens to the page cache on a filter change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the list network-only or network+DB (RemoteMediator)? Are filters combined server-side? Should scroll position persist per filter? Do filter changes need to be shareable via deep link? What's the paging key (offset vs cursor)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Debounce the slider and distinctUntilChanged the filter object so 40 requests become ~1 per drag end. That addresses the load; ordering bug fix follows from the pipeline.
  3. Hypotheses (for stale results), ranked: manual loads race without cancellation; two PagingSources alive; collecting PagingData in a scope that outlives the filter change; cachedIn applied before the filter switch (caching the wrong stream).
  4. How I'd verify: log filter hash + PagingSource instance id on every load(); Layout Inspector isn't useful here, use Paging's LoadState logging; a test with TestPager/asSnapshot (paging-testing) and a fake source that delays older filters.
  5. Design:
filters (StateFlow<Filter>, in SavedStateHandle)
   -> debounce only on the slider-driven part
   -> distinctUntilChanged
   -> flatMapLatest { f -> Pager(config) { CatalogPagingSource(api, f) }.flow }   // new PagingSource per filter
   -> cachedIn(viewModelScope)                                                   // AFTER flatMapLatest
   -> UI: collectAsLazyPagingItems()
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class, FlowPreview::class)
class CatalogViewModel(private val repo: CatalogRepo, saved: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {

    private val filter = MutableStateFlow(Filter())          // restore from `saved` as needed
    private val priceDraft = MutableStateFlow(filter.value.price)

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            priceDraft.debounce(250).collect { p -> filter.update { it.copy(price = p) } }   // atomic update
        }
    }

    val items: Flow<PagingData<Listing>> = filter
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .flatMapLatest { f ->
            Pager(PagingConfig(pageSize = 30, prefetchDistance = 10, enablePlaceholders = false)) {
                CatalogPagingSource(repo, f)
            }.flow
        }
        .cachedIn(viewModelScope)

    fun onSlider(p: PriceRange) { priceDraft.value = p }
    fun onCategory(c: Category) = filter.update { it.copy(category = c) }
}

cachedIn after flatMapLatest caches the current paging stream so rotation resumes from the cached pages and position; a filter change creates a new PagingData generation, and the UI scrolls to top (correct behavior, since content changed). flatMapLatest cancels the old Pager flow, so stale pages cannot be delivered. Text search gets its own debounce(300); chips/toggles apply instantly (no debounce). A PagingSource.getRefreshKey should map the anchor to a key so refresh after invalidation keeps position (cursor-based: key from the anchor item). 6. Fix path: replace manual loads incrementally behind a flag; keep the repo returning Result so PagingSource.load maps errors to LoadResult.Error (retry button) and never throws raw exceptions. 7. Prevention: paging-testing (asSnapshot { scrollTo(...) }) tests: apply filter A then B quickly and assert only B's items; rotation test (recreate VM scope not needed, test cachedIn through TestScope); trace for p95 first page; log 'filter -> request' counts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: With RemoteMediator + Room, filtering would run in SQL against the cached table; at 2M listings I would not cache the full catalog, only visited pages with TTL. I'd not hold PagingData in StateFlow (stateIn on PagingData is wrong; cachedIn is the API). Not Pager creation inside the composable (new pager per recomposition).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Filter changes while a page is loading?" → The old PagingSource is invalidated/collection cancelled; the in-flight request is cancelled if it is a suspend Retrofit call (cooperative cancellation reaches OkHttp Call.cancel).
  • "Preserve scroll position per filter?" → Keep a Map<Filter, Int> in the VM and restore after the new generation loads; usually not worth it.
  • "Two Pagers on one screen (tabs)?" → Each tab VM/scope has its own cachedIn, and Pager instances must not be shared across different filters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The "1 in 300" stale-result bug was a manual launch per filter change on a Dispatchers.IO pool with no cancellation. It vanished in the first hour of the Paging migration and the team deleted a 400-line hand-rolled pagination helper.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: manual page loading with mutable lists.
  • Hire: flatMapLatest + Pager + cachedIn(viewModelScope), debounce on slider.
  • Strong hire: cachedIn placement reasoning, getRefreshKey, LoadResult.Error mapping, paging-testing, atomic filter updates, RemoteMediator trade-off.

questions.contextHtml:
Home screen loads six independent sections (banners, recommendations, orders, wallet, offers, notifications). Cold-start-to-content p95 is 3.9 s on mid-range devices; users on bad networks often see a blank screen for 10+ s. One flaky endpoint (offers, 8% error rate and sometimes 20 s hangs) is blamed. Code:

suspend fun loadHome(): HomeData = coroutineScope {
    val banners = async { api.banners() }
    val recs    = async { api.recommendations() }
    val orders  = async { api.orders() }
    val wallet  = async { api.wallet() }
    val offers  = async { api.offers() }
    val notifs  = async { api.notifications() }
    HomeData(banners.await(), recs.await(), orders.await(), wallet.await(), offers.await(), notifs.await())
}

Crashlytics also shows a rare crash: JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling surfacing in the UI as an error toast.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why one failing endpoint blanks the entire screen, and redesign for partial results, bounded latency, and correct error reporting.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap each in try/catch." The try/catch around await() does not prevent the sibling cancellation in coroutineScope, because the failed async has already cancelled the parent scope. Also nothing bounds the 20 s hang.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which sections are critical (wallet?) vs optional? Is stale cached data acceptable? What's the latency budget per section? Can the server provide an aggregate endpoint?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Per-section timeouts (e.g. 3 s optional sections) and fallback to cache; ship server-side flag to disable offers temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) structured concurrency: first failing child cancels the scope and siblings (by design); (b) no timeouts, so a hung call holds awaitAll; (c) sequential await order hides which one failed; (d) JobCancellationException surfacing because a sibling's cancellation is caught by a generic catch (e: Exception) upstream and displayed.
  4. How I'd verify: Network profiler timeline per call; unit test with a fake API: one async throws, assert others are cancelled; log which section failed with a tag; reproduce with a delayed MockWebServer response.
  5. Root cause: In coroutineScope { async {...} }, a child failure cancels the parent scope, which cancels the siblings: this is the all-or-nothing contract, great for atomic operations and wrong for independent sections. The exception rethrown by coroutineScope is the original; the Parent job is Cancelling one is what the siblings see, and if code catches generic Exception and renders it, you display the wrong error.
  6. Fix: Model sections as independent results; each section failure isolated; bound each by time; render progressively.
sealed interface Section<out T> {
    data object Loading : Section<Nothing>
    data class Ready<T>(val data: T, val stale: Boolean = false) : Section<T>
    data class Failed(val error: Throwable) : Section<Nothing>
}

private suspend fun <T> section(timeoutMs: Long, cached: suspend () -> T?, call: suspend () -> T): Section<T> =
    try {
        Section.Ready(withTimeout(timeoutMs) { call() })
    } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {            // must be caught BEFORE the generic CancellationException rule
        cached()?.let { Section.Ready(it, stale = true) } ?: Section.Failed(e)
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e                                            // real cancellation: propagate
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        cached()?.let { Section.Ready(it, stale = true) } ?: Section.Failed(e)
    }

fun homeState(): Flow<HomeState> = channelFlow {
    val state = MutableStateFlow(HomeState())
    launch { state.collect { send(it) } }
    supervisorScope {                                      // independent children
        launch { val b = section(3_000, ::cachedBanners) { api.banners() }; state.update { it.copy(banners = b) } }
        launch { val w = section(5_000, ::cachedWallet)  { api.wallet() };  state.update { it.copy(wallet = w) } }
        // ...other four
    }
}

Key points: supervisorScope (or async inside it) gives independence; StateFlow.update is atomic so concurrent completions do not lose each other's writes (compare with state.value = state.value.copy(...), a lost-update race). TimeoutCancellationException extends CancellationException, so a blanket "rethrow CancellationException" would break timeouts: catch it first (or use withTimeoutOrNull). With supervisorScope + async, exceptions surface at await(), so always await or wrap in a Result inside the async. 7. Prevention: tests with runTest + advanceTimeBy for each timeout; fault-injection (per-endpoint chaos) in QA builds; an SLO per section; code-review rule "independent UI sections never share a coroutineScope". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not runCatching around await() alone. Not a single awaitAll() for UI that can render progressively. Also consider a BFF/aggregate endpoint: fewer connections on mobile and consistent errors, but a server-team dependency; client-side fan-out is the pragmatic first step. Keep concurrency bounded on very slow networks (6 parallel calls compete for bandwidth; HTTP/2 multiplexes over one connection, which helps).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Critical section fails, but others succeeded?" → Per-section state still; screen-level policy decides (show error card in that section with retry).
  • "Why not async with CoroutineExceptionHandler?" → A handler on async does nothing: exceptions are thrown at await; handlers only apply to root launch-style coroutines.
  • "Cold-start budget?" → Show cached HomeState from Room immediately (stale-while-revalidate), then merge fresh sections.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One 'offers' hang affected every home-screen user for two days because it was logically optional but structurally mandatory. The code fix was 30 lines; agreeing on which sections were optional took a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: try/catch around awaits; doesn't know siblings are cancelled.
  • Hire: supervisorScope + timeouts + per-section state.
  • Strong hire: TimeoutCancellationException subtlety, atomic update, async exception semantics, stale-cache fallback, progressive rendering, testing with virtual time.

questions.contextHtml: PM: "Make the feed feel instant, but never show wrong data." Feed has 20 items per page, data changes every few minutes server-side, average user opens the app 5x/day. Current behavior: always show a spinner until the network responds (p50 700 ms, p95 2.6 s, offline = error screen). Engineering has Room, Retrofit, Flow. The PM cannot define "wrong" precisely; some items are price-sensitive (cannot be stale > 5 minutes), others are editorial.
questions.promptHtml: Turn this ambiguity into a concrete design: caching policy, Flow shape, refresh triggers, error states, and how you'd prove it's better.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Load from DB first, then network." Without addressing staleness rules, duplicate emissions, error when offline, or how the UI knows data is stale vs fresh.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields are price-sensitive and what's their max age? Is it OK to show stale data with a visible "updated 3 min ago"? What does "wrong" cost (checkout mismatch vs cosmetic)? Can the server send ETag/updatedAt/ttl per item? Is there personalization (cache per user)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (no incident); smallest first step is "show the last cached feed immediately with a subtle refreshing indicator", for the editorial portion, measured via A/B.
  3. Hypotheses (risks): stale price shown at checkout; cache-key collisions across users/locales; double-emission flicker (cached -> network replacing items with a different order); refresh storms on every screen entry.
  4. How I'd verify: an A/B test: time-to-content p50/p95, scroll-depth, bounce, and "price mismatch at checkout" rate as a guardrail metric; instrumentation of cache age at render.
  5. Design (concrete):
UI state = DB (single source of truth) + RefreshState
Policy:  editorial rows: show cache regardless of age (<= 24 h), refresh if older than 5 min on app start
         price-sensitive: show cached price only if age <= 5 min, otherwise render item with price placeholder
         always: refresh on pull-to-refresh and on connectivity regained
Errors:  network error + cache present -> keep showing cache + non-blocking banner; no cache -> full error with retry
class FeedRepository(private val dao: FeedDao, private val api: FeedApi, private val clock: Clock) {

    fun feed(): Flow<FeedUi> = combine(dao.observeFeed(), refreshState) { rows, rs ->
        FeedUi(
            items = rows.map { it.toUi(priceFresh = clock.millis() - it.fetchedAt <= 300_000) },
            refreshing = rs is Refreshing,
            error = (rs as? Failed)?.takeIf { rows.isEmpty() }?.error,
            lastUpdated = rows.maxOfOrNull { it.fetchedAt },
        )
    }

    private val refreshState = MutableStateFlow<RefreshState>(Idle)
    private val refreshMutex = Mutex()

    suspend fun refresh(force: Boolean = false) {
        if (!refreshMutex.tryLock()) return                   // single-flight refresh
        try {
            val newest = dao.newestFetchedAt() ?: 0L
            if (!force && clock.millis() - newest < 60_000) return
            refreshState.value = Refreshing
            val page = api.feed()                              // cancellable suspend call
            dao.replaceFeed(page.map { it.toEntity(clock.millis()) })   // @Transaction
            refreshState.value = Idle
        } catch (e: CancellationException) { refreshState.value = Idle; throw e }
        catch (e: Exception) { refreshState.value = Failed(e) }
        finally { refreshMutex.unlock() }
    }
}

ViewModel: init { viewModelScope.launch { repo.refresh() } } plus repo.feed().stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), FeedUi.Loading). Items diffed by stable id so the cached -> fresh swap animates instead of flickering; the DB write is in a transaction so UI never sees a half-replaced list. Flow is driven by the DB, so the refresh result arrives via the same stream: no separate "network emission" path to reconcile. 6. Fix path: ship cache-first for editorial only; add price freshness rule second; expand after guardrail metrics are flat. 7. Prevention: tests with a fake Clock; DB migration for fetchedAt; logging cache age; per-user cache key (clear on logout!); kill-switch via remote config. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "cache then network" as two emissions with different sources in the UI (reconciliation bugs). Not infinite TTL. Not caching authenticated user data across accounts (clear DB on logout, or key by user id). HTTP-level cache (OkHttp Cache + Cache-Control) could cover some of this with zero code but cannot express per-field freshness or offline UI state; I'd use it for images and idempotent static GETs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Pull-to-refresh spam?" → tryLock single-flight plus the 60 s freshness guard unless force.
  • "Cache grows unbounded?" → Prune on write (keep last N pages / 7 days), run in the same transaction.
  • "What if refresh takes longer than the user stays on-screen?" → Run in viewModelScope (cancelled with the VM), or app scope if the result should still land in the DB; DB writes are cheap to keep.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-meaning cache-first rollout showed yesterday's flash-sale prices for a few seconds after launch. Splitting freshness rules by field type, with the price rule enforced at render time, kept the speedup and removed the complaints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "DB first then network" with no rules.
  • Hire: DB as single source, freshness policy, offline fallback, error states.
  • Strong hire: turns ambiguity into explicit rules and metrics, single-flight refresh, transactional replace, per-user cache keys, guardrail-metric A/B.

questions.contextHtml: Analytics SDK wrapper in a streaming app. Today: each event does scope.launch { api.send(event) }, ~15 events/min/user. Product will add player telemetry: ~4 events/second during playback (peak 600K concurrent players). Backend asks for batches (max 50 events or 5 s, whichever first), gzip, and no loss on app kill (best-effort). Currently 2-3% of events are lost, and we've seen OutOfMemoryError in the SDK on low-end devices after long offline periods. Battery team complains about radio wakeups.
questions.promptHtml: Design the client pipeline for 10x the event rate. Cover buffering, flush policy, backpressure, persistence, and coroutines/Flow structure.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Channel.UNLIMITED plus a loop that sends whatever it receives. Unbounded memory, no flush by time, no persistence, a failed batch drops events or blocks forever.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which events are loss-intolerant (purchases) vs lossy (progress ticks)? Max acceptable delay? Server dedupe by event id? Is there an event schema version? Max local storage budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the in-memory queue (OOM) with a drop-oldest policy for low-priority events and persist high-priority ones synchronously to Room/file; stop per-event launch.
  3. Hypotheses (for the 2-3% loss), ranked: process death with in-flight launch; failed sends not retried; unbounded concurrency causing 429s; events dropped on trySend failure.
  4. How I'd verify: monotonic sequence number per session + server gap detection; kill-process tests; Network profiler for radio wakeups; heap dump for the queue.
  5. Design:
track(event) -> Channel<Event>(capacity=1000, onBufferOverflow=DROP_OLDEST)   // hot path never blocks UI
   -> single consumer coroutine: batch by (50 items | 5 s)
   -> persist batch to Room (WAL) -> sender coroutine takes oldest batch -> gzip -> POST -> delete on ack
   -> failure: exponential backoff (cap 5 min), keep batch; storage cap 5 MB, drop-oldest lowest priority
   -> app background: flush attempt via WorkManager one-time work
class EventPipeline(scope: CoroutineScope, private val store: BatchStore, private val api: IngestApi) {

    private val inbox = Channel<Event>(capacity = 1_000, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)

    fun track(e: Event) { inbox.trySend(e) }               // non-suspending; never blocks callers

    init {
        scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
            val buf = ArrayList<Event>(50)
            while (isActive) {
                // wait for the first event, then collect up to 50 or until 5s from the first one
                buf += inbox.receive()
                withTimeoutOrNull(5_000) {
                    while (buf.size < 50) buf += inbox.receive()
                }
                store.save(buf.toList()); buf.clear()
            }
        }
        scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { sendLoop() }
    }

    private suspend fun sendLoop() {
        var attempt = 0
        while (true) {
            val batch = store.oldest() ?: run { store.awaitNew(); continue }
            val ok = runCatching { api.ingest(gzip(batch.json), batch.id) }   // batch.id = idempotency key
                .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
                .isSuccess
            if (ok) { store.delete(batch.id); attempt = 0 }
            else delay(minOf(300_000L, 1_000L shl minOf(attempt++, 8)))
        }
    }
}

Why the time-window loop works: withTimeoutOrNull(5_000) bounds the accumulation window from the first event, so a lone event is flushed in 5 s. Gotcha: when the timeout fires, a receive could be cancelled between dequeue and +=; Channel.receive is cancellation-atomic (an element is either received or not), so no loss. Equivalent Flow form: inbox.receiveAsFlow().chunked(50, 5.seconds) exists as a proposed/experimental-style operator not in the stable kotlinx.coroutines API as of my knowledge; verify before relying on it, or write the loop as above. Radio efficiency: batching 4 events/s into 1 request per 5 s (20 events) vs 4 requests/s is a 20x drop in requests; to go further, raise the window to 15-30 s for telemetry and piggyback on other traffic. 6. Fix path: dual-run old and new pipelines with a sequence number to compare counts; roll out by percentage. 7. Prevention: chaos tests (airplane mode for 30 min at 4 events/s = 7,200 events ~ at ~300 B each ≈ 2.2 MB, under the 5 MB cap); heap budget test; server-side gap alerts; sampling for high-frequency events (1 in N) to bound volume. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: DROP_OLDEST loses data under overload by design (document which event classes can drop); not UNLIMITED; not SharedFlow for this (it is for multicast, not durable queueing). Not one coroutine per event (cost is small per coroutine, ~tens of bytes, but 600K users x 4/s of unbounded concurrent HTTP is the real problem). Not sending from Dispatchers.Main. Not using WorkManager as the per-batch sender during playback (scheduling latency); use it only as the background flusher.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Two processes (service + app) produce events?" → One writer to the store (ContentProvider or a single process owns the pipeline), or store with per-process sequence IDs.
  • "Server wants ordering?" → Per-session sequence numbers plus server-side sort; batches carry min/max seq.
  • "Ack lost after successful send (duplicate batch)?" → Server dedupes on batch.id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An SDK upgrade replaced a bounded queue with an unbounded one "for reliability"; a week-long offline cohort grew a 300 MB in-memory list and crashed on resume. A bounded Channel and a disk store with a hard cap removed both the OOMs and the data-loss arguments.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: per-event launch or unbounded channel.
  • Hire: bounded channel, batching by size and time, backoff, persistence.
  • Strong hire: overflow policy by priority, cancellation-atomic receive reasoning, idempotent batch ids, storage budget math, radio/battery reasoning, rollout comparison.

questions.contextHtml: Leadership: "Cold start is slow, fix it." Data: cold start p50 2.4 s, p95 5.8 s on low-end devices (time to initial display, Play Console + Firebase Performance). Application.onCreate synchronously initializes 14 SDKs (~1.9 s total on a Moto G-class device), Firebase, DI graph, Crashlytics, analytics, an ads SDK, feature flags (blocking network read with 1 s timeout) and a runBlocking { dataStore.data.first() }. Someone proposes "just move everything into GlobalScope.launch".
questions.promptHtml: How do you approach this? What goes where, how do you use coroutines safely, and how do you prove improvement?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Dumps all init into GlobalScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default). This creates races (code using an SDK before init completes), loses crashes during init, ignores thread-safety requirements of SDKs, and doesn't measure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the metric (TTID, TTFD, "time to interactive")? Which SDKs must run on the main thread / before first screen (crash reporting, DI)? Which are needed for the first screen (flags, session)? Is a Baseline Profile in use? What's the device target?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the runBlocking read from onCreate and make the feature flag read non-blocking with a safe default; defer the ads SDK. These are low-risk and probably take 1 s off.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) sync SDK inits dominate (1.9 s); (b) runBlocking + flag read (~1 s worst case); (c) class loading/dex and no Baseline Profile (JIT); (d) heavy first-screen work (layout inflation, first network call).
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto/system trace with custom Trace.beginSection around each init; adb shell am start -W; Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric (cold) on a real low-end device; Android Studio CPU profiler startup recording; reportFullyDrawn() for TTFD.
  5. Plan (classify before parallelizing):
Tier 0 (must be sync, before first frame): crash reporting, DI root, StrictMode (debug)         ~150 ms
Tier 1 (needed for first screen; start early, await when needed):  feature flags, session/auth state
Tier 2 (not needed for first frame): analytics, ads, remote config refresh, image loader warm-up -> after first frame
class App : Application() {
    val appScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, t -> Crash.log(t) })
    lateinit var startup: Deferred<StartupState>

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Crash.init(this); Graph.init(this)                       // tier 0, sync
        startup = appScope.async {                                // tier 1 in parallel
            val flags = async { Flags.loadCachedOrDefault() }     // cached/default first, refresh later
            val session = async { Session.restore() }
            StartupState(flags.await(), session.await())
        }
    }

    // tier 2: called by the first Activity once its first frame is drawn (e.g. from a reportFullyDrawn() hook)
    fun onFirstFrame() {
        appScope.launch { Analytics.init(); Remote.refresh() }       // thread-agnostic SDKs
        Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).post { Ads.init(this) }      // main-thread-only SDK, deferred not parallelized
    }
}

Post-first-frame work is triggered explicitly by the first Activity, which is simple, testable and avoids guessing frame timing. SDKs that require the main thread (many ads SDKs) can't be moved to Default; defer them instead of parallelizing (withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { ads.init() } after first frame). First screen: val s = (application as App).startup.await() inside lifecycleScope (never block on it), showing the splash/skeleton until it completes. 6. Fix path: Ship in increments with measurement: (1) remove runBlocking, (2) tier-2 deferral, (3) parallelize tier 1, (4) Baseline Profile, (5) App Startup library for ordered initializers. Each as separate release with Macrobenchmark numbers in the PR. 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark in CI on a low-end device farm with regression gate (e.g., fail if p50 regresses > 10%); a rule that any new Application.onCreate init requires a tier and an owner; Play Console startup alerts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not GlobalScope (no exception handling, untestable, unowned). Not parallelizing SDKs with hidden thread assumptions without vendor confirmation. Not hiding cold-start with a long splash (hurts the metric honesty). Parallelism isn't free on 4 slow cores: contention with the main thread's own work, so measure; fewer, deferred inits beat many parallel ones.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not just Dispatchers.IO for everything?" → CPU-bound init competes for cores; IO is for blocking calls. Also several SDKs need the main looper.
  • "Race: the first screen calls Analytics.track before init?" → Provide a facade that queues until ready (a bounded buffer), not lateinit access.
  • "How do you measure 'improved'?" → Macrobenchmark percentiles over 10+ iterations plus field data (p50/p95 TTID) after rollout, not a single local run.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team moved all init off the main thread and cold start dropped 40% in the lab, then crash-free fell 0.3% in production because a feature used an SDK before its async init completed on slow devices. The tiering and an init-gate facade fixed both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: GlobalScope everything.
  • Hire: measures first, tiers init work, removes runBlocking, uses async/await for dependencies.
  • Strong hire: Perfetto/Macrobenchmark evidence, main-thread-only SDK handling, facade queuing, regression gates, incremental rollout, honest metric choice.

questions.contextHtml:
A real-estate app uploads up to 30 photos (3-6 MB each) per listing. Complaints: uploads take ~8 minutes on LTE, the app crashes with OOM on 3 GB devices when the user selects 30 photos, one failed photo aborts the whole batch and discards the 17 already uploaded, and cancelling leaves orphaned server objects. Current code:

suspend fun uploadAll(uris: List<Uri>) = coroutineScope {
    uris.map { uri ->
        async(Dispatchers.IO) {
            val bytes = contentResolver.openInputStream(uri)!!.readBytes()   // full file in memory
            api.upload(bytes)
        }
    }.awaitAll()
}
questions.promptHtml: Redesign for throughput, memory, partial failure, retries, and cancellation. State your concurrency number and justify it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Limit to 5 parallel." Without a justification, streaming, per-item results, or cleanup; or recommends Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(5) as if it bounds network concurrency (it bounds threads, but a suspending network call doesn't hold a thread).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the server support resumable/multipart uploads? Must the user wait on screen (foreground) or can it continue in background? Image resizing allowed (do we need originals)? Order of photos required? Server cleanup API for orphans?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap concurrency at 3 and stream from disk now (OOM fix), and switch the batch from fail-fast to per-item results.
  3. Hypotheses (for slowness), ranked: 30 parallel uploads share one radio link, so each is slower and TCP congestion raises retransmits (no gain beyond 3-4 concurrent); 6 MB originals could be 1.5 MB after resize/compress; HTTP/1.1 connection limits (OkHttp default 5 per host) create queueing anyway; readBytes() memory churn and GC.
  4. How I'd verify: Network Profiler; time N uploads at concurrency 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 on throttled LTE (the throughput curve plateaus); heap profiler for readBytes; server metrics for orphans.
  5. Root cause: coroutineScope + async is fail-fast: one exception cancels siblings; readBytes plus 30 in-flight bodies = 30 x 6 MB = 180 MB; and cancellation of a coroutine doesn't undo server state.
  6. Fix:
sealed interface PhotoResult { data class Done(val uri: Uri, val remoteId: String) : PhotoResult
                               data class Failed(val uri: Uri, val error: Throwable) : PhotoResult }

fun uploadAll(uris: List<Uri>, parallelism: Int = 3): Flow<PhotoResult> = channelFlow {
    val gate = Semaphore(parallelism)
    supervisorScope {                                      // one failure doesn't kill siblings
        uris.forEach { uri ->
            launch {
                gate.withPermit {
                    val r = try {
                        PhotoResult.Done(uri, uploadWithRetry(uri))
                    } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
                    catch (e: Exception) { PhotoResult.Failed(uri, e) }
                    send(r)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

private suspend fun uploadWithRetry(uri: Uri): String {
    repeat(3) { attempt ->
        try {
            return api.upload(streamingBody(uri))         // RequestBody that reads in 64 KB chunks via ContentResolver
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            if (attempt == 2) throw e
            delay(1_000L shl attempt)
        }
    }
    error("unreachable")
}

streamingBody: a custom OkHttp RequestBody whose writeTo(sink) copies from contentResolver.openInputStream(uri) using source().use { sink.writeAll(it) }, so memory is O(buffer), not O(file). The Semaphore bounds in-flight uploads (the actual resource), whereas limitedParallelism bounds threads. Choice of 3: measured plateau, ~3 streams saturate typical LTE uplink (e.g., 15 Mbps up = ~1.9 MB/s; 30 x 4.5 MB = 135 MB takes ~72 s at full saturation vs 8 min today, so the 8 min figure shows the link is NOT saturated: handshake/serial overhead and retries dominate, and 3 streams recovers most of it). Add client-side downscale to max 2048 px / quality 85 (typically 4.5 MB -> ~0.8-1.2 MB), a bigger win than any concurrency tuning. Cancellation cleanup: track remoteIds uploaded in this batch in a local table; on user cancel call a best-effort DELETE for unattached objects from a withContext(NonCancellable) block, and have the server garbage-collect unattached objects after 24 h as the real safety net. Foreground/background: if uploads must survive the screen, run via WorkManager (setExpedited is quota-limited) with per-photo work chain or a CoroutineWorker that persists progress per photo in Room. 7. Prevention: MockWebServer tests: inject failure on photo 7; assert 29 succeed and 1 reports Failed; memory test with 30 x 6 MB fake streams; dashboards for upload success rate, median upload time per MB. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not unlimited async. Not retrying non-idempotent uploads without an idempotency key (a timeout after the server stored the file creates duplicates). Not readBytes(). Not compressing on the main thread (do it on Dispatchers.Default; decoding with inSampleSize/ImageDecoder to avoid a full-size bitmap).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Order must match the user's selection order?" → Upload in any order, assign sort index client-side and send it as metadata; display is by index.
  • "User kills the app at photo 12?" → Persist a per-photo state table; on relaunch/WorkManager resume only the pending ones using stable remote keys.
  • "Why not flatMapMerge(concurrency = 3)?" → Equivalent and more declarative: uris.asFlow().flatMapMerge(3) { flow { emit(upload(it)) } }; I prefer explicit Semaphore when I need per-item error handling and cleanup hooks. Both are valid.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Doubling concurrency from 3 to 6 made uploads slower on a carrier with aggressive uplink shaping. A dial-in config (server-driven parallelism) let us tune per network type without a release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: arbitrary parallelism limit, whole-file memory reads remain.
  • Hire: Semaphore/flatMapMerge bound, streaming body, per-item results with supervisorScope.
  • Strong hire: justifies concurrency with a measured plateau or math, handles cancellation cleanup and server GC, resizes images, idempotency and persistence for process death.

questions.contextHtml:
Delivery app, evening peak. Crash-free is fine but "app feels frozen": taps ok, yet screens show spinners for 10-20 s, p95 API-to-render jumped from 900 ms to 14 s on ~12% of sessions, mostly mid-range devices on Wi-Fi. No ANRs. A new "reconcile contacts" job was released that runs an 800-contact loop. Thread dump excerpt shows many threads:

"DefaultDispatcher-worker-23" ... Blocked
  at java.io.FileInputStream.readBytes
  at com.app.contacts.PhoneBook.hashAll(PhoneBook.kt:41)
  at com.app.contacts.Reconciler$run$2.invokeSuspend(Reconciler.kt:19)
"DefaultDispatcher-worker-64" ...

Reconciler.run does contacts.map { async(Dispatchers.IO) { hashAll(it) } }.awaitAll() and each hashAll does a blocking SQLite/file read and a 40 ms CPU hash. Also, other features use Dispatchers.IO for their own Room reads and SDK blocking calls.
questions.promptHtml: Why is unrelated work slowed? How do you diagnose and fix it with dispatcher design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Dispatchers.Default for CPU work." True but incomplete; doesn't understand the shared IO pool (default 64 threads cap), limitedParallelism views, nor why other features that aren't in the loop are blocked.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which operations run on Dispatchers.IO app-wide? Is any code using runBlocking/synchronized inside IO tasks? How many cores? Did this job run during startup?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-disable or throttle the reconcile job (feature flag), reduce its concurrency to 4; confirm p95 recovers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) IO pool saturation: Dispatchers.IO shares threads with Default and by default allows max(64, cores) threads. 800 async blocks of blocking reads create 64 busy threads; every other withContext(IO) call (Room, file) queues behind them.
    • (b) CPU-bound hashing on IO threads competes with Default for cores (IO threads are extra threads, but cores are fixed, so mid-range 6-8 cores are oversubscribed at 64 busy threads).
    • (c) SQLite writer lock contention (single writer), serialized behind blocking readers.
    • (d) Network stack starved (red herring: OkHttp uses its own dispatcher threads, not the coroutines pool).
  4. How I'd verify: thread dump counts of DefaultDispatcher-worker-* in state RUNNABLE/BLOCKED; Perfetto thread states (CPU scheduling latency, runnable-queued time); Android Studio CPU Profiler system trace; kotlinx-coroutines-debug DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() to see how many coroutines queued; a synthetic test that runs reconcile, then times an unrelated withContext(IO) { dao.get() }.
  5. Root cause: A shared, capped resource without a per-feature budget. Coroutine launch is cheap; blocking threads are not. 800 concurrent blocking tasks monopolise the 64-thread IO cap, so queued tasks from all other features wait. Math: 800 tasks x ~60 ms (20 ms I/O + 40 ms CPU) = 48 s of work; with 64 threads on 6 cores the CPU part alone is 800 x 40 ms = 32 s / 6 cores ~ 5.3 s of fully saturated cores, plus I/O wait, during which everything else is delayed by seconds: consistent with 10-14 s p95 on a slow device with thermal throttling.
  6. Fix:
object Dispatchers2 {
    // Own budgets: limitedParallelism views cap concurrent tasks per feature (IO views may add threads beyond the shared 64 cap)
    val contacts: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(2)
    val hashing: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)   // leave cores for the UI/render path
    val db: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(8)              // Room has its own executors; this is for non-Room blocking calls
}

suspend fun run(items: List<Contact>) = coroutineScope {
    items.chunked(50).forEach { batch ->                       // bounded work in flight, also yields between batches
        val results = batch.map { c ->
            async(Dispatchers2.contacts) { read(c) }           // blocking IO, 2 at a time
        }.awaitAll()
        withContext(Dispatchers2.hashing) { results.forEach { hash(it); ensureActive() } }
    }
}

limitedParallelism(n) (introduced as experimental in kotlinx.coroutines 1.6; I believe it was stabilized in 1.9, check the release notes for your version) gives a view that runs at most n tasks concurrently on the parent pool; views of Dispatchers.IO are not limited by the 64-thread IO cap itself, so each limited view has its own capacity budget without starving the shared pool (documented behavior for IO views). Splitting reads (IO, 2 wide) from CPU hashing (Default, 1 wide) matches each task to its resource. Lower priority: also use yield()/ensureActive() in long loops, and run the whole job as a deferrable WorkManager job (requiresDeviceIdle, requiresBatteryNotLow) instead of during peak foreground usage. 7. Prevention: inject dispatchers (never hard-code Dispatchers.IO) so budgets are central and tests use StandardTestDispatcher; a custom lint/detekt rule for Dispatchers.IO in feature code ("InjectDispatcher" rule exists in detekt's coroutines set); metrics: queue time on dispatcher (wrap tasks with timestamps); performance test that loads the app while the heavy job runs. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not newFixedThreadPoolContext per feature (real threads, never closed = leak; it's @DelicateCoroutinesApi). Not increasing kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism system property as the fix (it raises the cap and the oversubscription; it can be right for truly wait-bound workloads). Not Dispatchers.Default for blocking reads (starves CPU work; Default has only core-count threads).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does limitedParallelism(1) on a view not guarantee a single thread?" → It guarantees at most one task at a time, but successive tasks may run on different threads; don't rely on thread identity (use for mutual exclusion of coroutine work, not thread-local state).
  • "Room already has its own executor, so why does withContext(IO) matter for Room?" → Room's suspend DAOs hop to Room's query/transaction executors; wrapping in IO again is redundant. Non-Room blocking calls (files, SDKs) still need an IO budget.
  • "How would you detect starvation in production?" → Periodically post a no-op task to Dispatchers.IO and measure queue latency; report p95; alert above 200 ms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "background" contacts matcher quietly consumed the whole IO pool during the evening peak. The fix wasn't clever: a limitedParallelism(2) view and moving the job to idle-time WorkManager, plus a queue-latency metric that caught the next offender within a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "move to Default".
  • Hire: knows IO is a shared bounded pool, bounds concurrency, injects dispatchers.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the starvation, separates blocking from CPU budgets via limitedParallelism views, knows version status of the API, proposes queue-latency monitoring and WorkManager scheduling.

questions.subtopic: Optimistic updates with ordering and rollback
questions.contextHtml:
Grocery app cart, 900K DAU. Users tap "+" quickly (3-6 taps in 2 s). Each tap does an optimistic UI increment and fires PUT /cart/items/{id} with the new quantity. Support tickets: cart shows 4 but checkout has 2 (about 0.6% of carts with edits). Server logs show requests arriving out of order (qty=3 processed after qty=4). A failed request (5xx) currently reverts the UI to the quantity before that tap, producing flicker and wrong numbers. Code:

fun increment(itemId: String) {
    val newQty = (cart.value[itemId] ?: 0) + 1
    cart.update { it + (itemId to newQty) }               // optimistic
    viewModelScope.launch {
        try { api.setQty(itemId, newQty) }
        catch (e: Exception) { cart.update { it + (itemId to newQty - 1) } }   // rollback
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bugs and design a correct approach. What are the options for ordering, and which do you choose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a debounce." That reduces requests but doesn't fix out-of-order or rollback semantics, and a debounce loses the last update if the screen closes within the window.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the API accept absolute quantity (idempotent) or deltas? Does the server send a cart version/ETag? Is "last write wins by arrival" the server rule? Should the cart sync survive leaving the screen?

  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the API call idempotent and absolute (already setQty), add a client sequence number header so the server can ignore stale ones, and stop the wrong rollbacks.

  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) independent launch per tap: concurrent HTTP calls reorder on the network (different connections, retries); (b) rollback computes newQty - 1 from a stale closure, not the last confirmed state; (c) the VM scope cancels in-flight calls when the user navigates, leaving the server behind the UI; (d) race on cart.value read-then-update (read outside update).

  4. How I'd verify: Logging request seq + timestamps + server receive order; reproduce with MockWebServer delaying even-numbered requests; a runTest test that issues 5 taps and asserts the final server state.

  5. Root cause: Optimistic UI without a single ordered writer. Requests are concurrent commands over an unordered medium; the rollback logic assumes serial success.

  6. Fix options:

    • (1) Serialize per item: one worker per itemId consuming a Channel (actor-style); requests are sent in order. Simple, strong ordering, but N sequential round trips.
    • (2) Coalesce (latest wins) per item: keep a desired quantity map; a single sync loop sends only the latest desired value per item, skipping intermediate values. Fewest requests, correct final state, no ordering problem because intermediate values are irrelevant for absolute updates.
    • (3) Server versioning: send If-Match: <cart version>; on 409 refetch. Needed anyway for multi-device carts.

    I choose (2) plus (3): the UI shows desired state; a sync loop reconciles confirmed state toward it.

class CartSync(private val api: CartApi, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val desired = MutableStateFlow<Map<String, Int>>(emptyMap())      // what UI shows
    private val confirmed = MutableStateFlow<Map<String, Int>>(emptyMap())    // what server acked
    val display: StateFlow<Map<String, Int>> = desired

    fun set(itemId: String, qty: Int) = desired.update { it + (itemId to qty) }   // atomic

    init {
        scope.launch {
            desired.collectLatest { want ->                       // newest desired state restarts the sync pass
                delay(150)                                         // tiny coalescing window; cancelled by next tap
                val diff = want.filter { (id, q) -> confirmed.value[id] != q }
                for ((id, q) in diff) {
                    try {
                        api.setQty(id, q)
                        confirmed.update { it + (id to q) }
                    } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
                    catch (e: Exception) {
                        desired.update { it + (id to (confirmed.value[id] ?: 0)) }   // roll back to LAST CONFIRMED
                        emitError(e)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Caveat: collectLatest cancels the in-flight api.setQty when a new tap arrives; for a non-idempotent server that could leave an unknown state, but for absolute PUT it is safe; if cancellation mid-request is unacceptable, wrap the call in withContext(NonCancellable), at the cost of a delayed latest value. The sync scope must outlive the screen: inject an app/session scope so a user leaving mid-sync doesn't strand the server (and flush on onCleared). 7. Prevention: model-based test: generate random tap sequences with random per-request delays/failures; invariant: final confirmed == desired or UI shows an error with desired == confirmed. Metrics: cart mismatch rate between client display at checkout and server total; a pre-checkout "sync barrier" (awaitSettled()) that waits for desired == confirmed (with timeout) before starting payment. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rollback by arithmetic (- 1). Not serializing every tap through a single global queue (a slow item blocks others). Not debounce alone. Not relying on arrival order at the server without versions. Option (1) is better when operations are non-idempotent commands (e.g., "add coupon"), where dropping intermediates is wrong.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "User quits the app between tap and ack?" → Persist desired state (Room) and let the outbox/WorkManager reconcile on next launch.
  • "Why update { } rather than value = value + ...?" → update is a compare-and-set loop; the plain form can lose a concurrent write.
  • "Checkout button tapped while syncing?" → Disable or awaitSettled with a spinner and a 3 s timeout, then show the server's authoritative cart.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The mismatch only appeared above ~150 ms RTT, so QA on office Wi-Fi never saw it. The fix that mattered wasn't the code but the invariant "UI = desired, server = confirmed, reconcile loop connects them".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debounce only; arithmetic rollback.
  • Hire: serialize or coalesce updates; rollback to confirmed state.
  • Strong hire: desired/confirmed model, idempotency and versioning analysis, collectLatest cancellation caveat, scope lifetime, pre-checkout barrier, property-based tests.

questions.subtopic: Lost updates in StateFlow state reduction
questions.contextHtml:
A screen uses a single UiState data class in a MutableStateFlow. Several coroutines update parts of it: profile loaded, notifications count (from a Flow), a "dismiss banner" action, and a refresh result. Users report that the banner sometimes reappears after dismissing, and occasionally the profile is "empty" until the next refresh (~0.5% of sessions). Code:

data class UiState(
    val profile: Profile? = null,
    val unread: Int = 0,
    val bannerVisible: Boolean = true,
    val loading: Boolean = false,
)

class HomeViewModel(private val repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch { repo.unread().collect { _state.value = _state.value.copy(unread = it) } }
        refresh()
    }

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = _state.value.copy(loading = true)
        val p = repo.profile()                                   // 300-1500 ms
        _state.value = _state.value.copy(profile = p, loading = false)
    }

    fun dismissBanner() { _state.value = _state.value.copy(bannerVisible = false) }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the race, explain why it is rare, and fix it. Then explain what you would change if there were 12 such fields and 5 writers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "StateFlow is thread-safe so it's fine." The individual value get/set is atomic; the read-modify-write sequence is not.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What dispatcher do the writers run on (Main vs Default)? Is repo.unread() emitting on a background thread? Does the app intentionally allow concurrent writers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace all _state.value = _state.value.copy(...) with _state.update { it.copy(...) }.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lost update from non-atomic read-modify-write when writers run on different threads (e.g., unread() upstream or flowOn pushes work to Default); (b) stale captured state used after a suspension (here the copy is evaluated after the suspending profile() returns, which is actually fine, but code that read _state.value before the call and copied afterwards would overwrite newer changes); (c) dismissBanner persisted nowhere, so a process restart resets it (red herring for the symptom but a real product bug); (d) two refresh coroutines overlapping, an older one finishing last.
  4. How I'd verify: a stress test: 2 threads each doing 100,000 copy increments on a counter field with .value = vs .update {}; the former finishes with a total less than 200,000. In production, add a debug log of state transitions with writer name.
  5. Root cause: StateFlow.value read and write are each atomic, but value = value.copy(...) is two operations. If writer A reads state S0, then writer B writes S1 (banner dismissed), then A writes S0.copy(unread = n), B's change is lost: the banner reappears. When both writers are on the Main thread (e.g. viewModelScope default Dispatchers.Main.immediate), races can still occur around suspension points, but are much rarer, which explains why it's about 0.5% of sessions: the race needs the unread collector's copy and dismissBanner's write to interleave across threads or across a dispatch.
  6. Fix:
init {
    viewModelScope.launch { repo.unread().collect { n -> _state.update { it.copy(unread = n) } } }
    refresh()
}

private var refreshJob: Job? = null
fun refresh() {
    refreshJob?.cancel()                                          // newest refresh wins
    refreshJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
        try {
            val p = repo.profile()
            _state.update { it.copy(profile = p, loading = false) }
        } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
        catch (e: Exception) { _state.update { it.copy(loading = false) } }
    }
}

fun dismissBanner() = _state.update { it.copy(bannerVisible = false) }

update {} loops with compareAndSet and re-runs the lambda on contention, so the lambda must be pure and cheap (no side effects, because it can run more than once). The 12-field/5-writer case: split into independent flows owned by their sources and combine once:

val state: StateFlow<UiState> = combine(profileFlow, unreadFlow, bannerFlow, loadingFlow) { p, u, b, l ->
    UiState(p, u, b, l)
}.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState())

Each writer owns its own field, so there is nothing to race on, and combine derives the aggregate. If actions dominate (an MVI-style reducer), funnel intents through one Channel and a single reducer coroutine (scan), so there is exactly one writer. 7. Prevention: lint/detekt custom rule or code-review rule: ban _state.value = _state.value...; a stress test for the VM (multi-threaded Dispatchers.Default writers); keep reducers pure. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not synchronized blocks around value mutation (works but is easy to miss, and blocking in coroutines is a smell). Not making UiState mutable. Combining many flows has a small cost: combine emits when any source changes, so keep sources distinctUntilChanged.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Does Dispatchers.Main.immediate make the original code safe?" → Largely, for writers all on Main, because there is no preemption between the read and the write in a single synchronous block. But safety then depends on every writer staying on Main, which is a fragile invariant; update removes the dependence.
  • "Where do Mutex-guarded updates fit?" → When the update itself must suspend (call a suspend function between read and write); update can't suspend. Otherwise prefer update.
  • "Can update livelock?" → Only under extreme contention with a slow lambda; in practice no.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The bug was invisible in QA because every test ran on Dispatchers.Main via setMain(UnconfinedTestDispatcher()), so writers could never interleave. A stress test on Dispatchers.Default reproduced it in under a second.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "StateFlow is thread safe".
  • Hire: identifies the read-modify-write and uses update.
  • Strong hire: explains why it is rare, the purity requirement of update, per-owner state composition via combine, single-reducer alternative, and the test-dispatcher blind spot.

questions.contextHtml:
Live-trading-style screen in a fintech/sports app: a WebSocket pushes ~3,000 price updates per second across 400 instruments. The watchlist (30 visible symbols) is a Compose LazyColumn. On mid-range devices the UI drops to 11 fps, Choreographer logs "Skipped 87 frames", and memory climbs by ~40 MB/min until GC thrashes. Three screens collect the same stream. Code:

class PriceRepo(socket: PriceSocket, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    val prices: SharedFlow<Tick> = socket.ticks()                         // Flow<Tick>
        .shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 0)
}
// ViewModel
val rows = prices.scan(emptyMap<String, Tick>()) { acc, t -> acc + (t.symbol to t) }   // copies the whole map per tick
    .map { it.values.sortedBy(Tick::symbol) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Lazily, emptyList())

socket.ticks() is a callbackFlow { ... trySend(tick) ... awaitClose{} } (default buffer).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the symptoms mechanically and fix the pipeline end to end.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add buffer()" or "use conflate()" without noticing the O(n) map copy per tick, the subscriber-side sort, per-symbol coalescing, or that SharedFlow with a slow subscriber suspends the emitter.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What display rate is needed (humans can't read 3,000/s; 4-10 Hz per visible row is plenty)? Do all consumers need every tick (charts, alerts) or just the latest price? Is order of ticks per symbol important for charts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side throttle or subscribe only to visible symbols; client: sample the UI stream to ~100-250 ms; remove the full-map copy from the hot path. Together these should remove the frame drops immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-tick allocation: acc + pair creates a new LinkedHashMap of up to 400 entries per tick: 3,000 x 400 = 1.2M entry copies/s plus sort; this causes GC churn (the memory climb); (b) StateFlow emission + recomposition at 3,000/s: StateFlow conflates, but the upstream scan/sort work still runs for every tick; (c) shareIn(replay=0, buffer default 64): with a slow collector the emitter suspends or, under callbackFlow default buffer, trySend fails if the channel is full (BUFFERED = 64), silently dropping ticks; (d) three collectors triplicate work if each has its own scan.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto frame timeline and Android Studio Memory Profiler allocation tracking (hot allocation site is LinkedHashMap.put), Compose Layout Inspector recomposition counts, JankStats; log trySend result failures.
  5. Root cause: An unbounded-rate producer feeding per-event heavy work on the consumer path, and no coalescing stage that matches the stream's semantics ("latest price per symbol wins"). Backpressure behavior was accidental: callbackFlow defaults to a 64-slot buffer (Channel.BUFFERED); on overflow, trySend fails and the tick is dropped at random, not by policy.
  6. Fix:
class PriceRepo(socket: PriceSocket, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    // 1. Producer: explicit policy, coalesce at the edge
    private val ticks: Flow<Tick> = callbackFlow {
        val l = socket.listen { t -> trySend(t) }
        awaitClose { l.close() }
    }.buffer(capacity = 1024, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)   // bounded and deliberate

    // 2. Latest-per-symbol snapshot, updated in place on ONE coroutine, published at 10 Hz
    val snapshot: StateFlow<Map<String, Tick>> = flow {
        val latest = HashMap<String, Tick>(512)                       // confined to this coroutine
        var lastEmit = 0L
        ticks.collect { t ->
            latest[t.symbol] = t
            val now = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()
            if (now - lastEmit >= 100) { lastEmit = now; emit(latest.toMap()) }   // copy once per 100 ms, not per tick
        }
    }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
     .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyMap())
}

// ViewModel: derive only what the screen shows
val rows: StateFlow<List<Row>> = combine(repo.snapshot, visibleSymbols) { snap, visible ->
    visible.mapNotNull { snap[it]?.toRow() }          // 30 rows, not 400
}.distinctUntilChanged()
 .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

Copy cost: 400 entries x 10 Hz = 4,000 entry copies/s versus 1.2M before, about 300x less. The mutable HashMap is safe because only the flow {} body touches it (single coroutine confinement); only immutable snapshots escape. WhileSubscribed stops the socket subscription when no screen is visible (and re-subscribes only visible symbols if the protocol supports it). In Compose use collectAsStateWithLifecycle(), stable key = symbol in LazyColumn, @Immutable/stable Row types, and derivedStateOf/per-row state so only changed rows recompose. Charts that need every tick should consume a separate, buffered branch, not the UI snapshot. 7. Prevention: JankStats + Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric scenario with a replayed 3,000 tick/s fixture; allocation budget test; a trySend failure counter (drops per second) on the dashboard; review rule: every hot stream has an explicit overflow policy and a rate budget. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: conflate() is right only when "latest wins" across the whole stream; here it would drop ticks for symbols other than the latest one, so coalescing must be per key. DROP_OLDEST on the producer buffer is acceptable for prices (stale values are worthless) but wrong for orders/fills. Not Channel.UNLIMITED (memory). Not sample(100) alone: it keeps only the last tick in the window, losing other symbols.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does SharedFlow with a slow subscriber stall everyone?" → With the default BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, emit suspends until the slowest subscriber has room, so a slow collector back-pressures the upstream and the other collectors; use DROP_OLDEST/conflate for lossy streams.
  • "Where did the 40 MB/min come from?" → Short-lived map copies; they are garbage-collectable, but at that rate they trigger frequent GC pauses (which are the real jank source) and memory climbs until GC catches up.
  • "How would you let a chart see every tick?" → A second consumer on ticks with buffer(DROP_OLDEST) and batch-draw per frame via withFrameNanos.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" the jank by moving the scan to Dispatchers.Default. Frame times improved a bit, then GC pauses on the same device class made it worse; the per-tick map copy was the real cost, and removing it did more than any threading change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "add buffer" or move work to a background thread.
  • Hire: per-key coalescing, rate-limited publishing, bounded buffer with explicit policy.
  • Strong hire: quantifies allocations, explains SharedFlow suspension semantics, thread confinement of the mutable map, Compose-side stability and recomposition control, and benchmarks with replayed load.

questions.subtopic: Resilience layer: timeouts, retries, circuit breaker
questions.contextHtml: Your org asks you to standardize network resilience across 15 feature teams. Today every team writes its own try/catch + retry. Incidents seen: (1) a retry-on-any-exception wrapper swallowed CancellationException, so screens kept loading after the user left (leaked work, 6% extra backend load); (2) a payment POST retried after a read timeout and double-charged; (3) during a backend brownout, 900K clients retried 3 times each, amplifying load 4x; (4) a withTimeout(5_000) around a Flow collector surfaced as a user-visible "Job was cancelled" error.
questions.promptHtml: Design a shared Resilience API in Kotlin. Cover timeouts, retries, idempotency, circuit-breaking, and the cancellation pitfalls. Explain the API surface and the defaults you'd choose.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: A retry(times = 3) { block() } helper with catch (e: Exception). It retries non-retryable errors, swallows cancellation, has no jitter/budget, and does not distinguish idempotent from non-idempotent calls.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints are idempotent (GET, PUT, keyed POST)? Does the server return Retry-After/429? Existing OkHttp interceptors/timeouts (connect/read/call)? Do teams need per-call overrides? Is there a server-side idempotency mechanism for payments?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Org-wide: set OkHttpClient.callTimeout, disable retryOnConnectionFailure for non-idempotent methods or ensure keys, and ban the ad-hoc helpers via lint. Stop the amplification: a retry budget (at most ~10% extra requests) rather than "3 per call".
  3. Hypotheses (the incident causes), ranked: catching Throwable/Exception without rethrowing cancellation; retry policy not tied to HTTP semantics; no jitter; no global brake; timeouts applied at the wrong layer (collector vs request).
  4. How I'd verify: replay incidents as tests (fake API that times out on first call and records requests; a test that cancels the caller mid-retry and asserts no further attempts; a brownout simulation with 10K fake clients).
  5. Design: one small, boring API with strong defaults:
sealed interface Idempotency { data object Safe : Idempotency; data class Keyed(val key: String) : Idempotency; data object Unsafe : Idempotency }

data class Policy(
    val timeoutMs: Long = 8_000,                       // per attempt
    val maxAttempts: Int = 3,
    val baseDelayMs: Long = 400,
    val maxDelayMs: Long = 8_000,
)

class Resilience(private val breaker: CircuitBreaker, private val budget: RetryBudget, private val rnd: Random = Random.Default) {

    suspend fun <T> call(idem: Idempotency, policy: Policy = Policy(), block: suspend () -> T): T {
        val attempts = if (idem is Idempotency.Unsafe) 1 else policy.maxAttempts      // never auto-retry unsafe
        var last: Throwable? = null
        repeat(attempts) { i ->
            breaker.checkOrThrow()                                                    // fail fast when open
            try {
                val r = withTimeout(policy.timeoutMs) { block() }
                breaker.onSuccess(); return r
            } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
                last = e; breaker.onFailure()                                         // our timeout: retryable
            } catch (e: CancellationException) {
                throw e                                                               // caller cancelled: never retry/swallow
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                if (!e.isRetryable()) throw e                                         // 4xx (except 408/429), parse errors, etc.
                last = e; breaker.onFailure()
            }
            if (i < attempts - 1) {
                if (!budget.tryAcquire()) throw last!!                                // global retry brake
                delay(backoffWithFullJitter(i, policy, (last as? HttpException)?.retryAfterMs()))
            }
        }
        throw last!!
    }

    private fun backoffWithFullJitter(i: Int, p: Policy, retryAfter: Long?): Long {
        val cap = minOf(p.maxDelayMs, p.baseDelayMs shl i)
        return maxOf(retryAfter ?: 0L, rnd.nextLong(0, cap + 1))
    }
}

Details that matter: (1) TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, so order of catch clauses is semantic: the timeout clause must come first, then the generic CancellationException rethrow. (2) withTimeout wraps one attempt, not the retry loop, so total time is bounded by attempts x timeout + delays; also expose a total deadline for user-facing calls. (3) For Unsafe calls (payment without a key) attempts = 1: the double-charge incident can't happen; for Keyed, retries are safe because the server dedupes. (4) The circuit breaker is a tiny state machine (Closed -> Open after N failures in a window -> HalfOpen after a cool-down allowing 1 probe), stored per host/endpoint-group, thread-safe via AtomicReference/Mutex; the UI shows cached data when open. (5) RetryBudget: token bucket refilled by successes (e.g., +0.1 token per success, max 10) so under brownout the retries stop automatically: this is what stops the 4x amplification. For the Flow case: apply timeouts to the upstream request (e.g., flow { emit(withTimeout(...) { api.get() }) }) or use timeout() operators carefully, not withTimeout around collect, which cancels the whole collection and surfaces TimeoutCancellationException to the UI. 6. Fix path: introduce as a library module, migrate payments and auth first (highest risk), then high-QPS reads; wire through Retrofit via a CallAdapter or at repository level; keep OkHttp's own connection-level retry disabled for POST. 7. Prevention: lint/detekt rule forbidding catch (e: Exception|Throwable) in suspend functions without a CancellationException rethrow (detekt has SuspendFunSwallowedCancellation in newer versions; otherwise custom); contract tests for the library; dashboards for breaker state, retry-budget exhaustion, attempts-per-request; load drills with injected 5xx. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not retry-everything defaults. Not a hand-rolled breaker if a vetted library fits (but on mobile, libraries are heavy and a 60-line version is acceptable; keep it well tested). Per-client breakers can't see global health, so they protect the backend only statistically; server-side load shedding and Retry-After are still required. Not hedged requests (duplicates load) except for idempotent, latency-critical reads, behind a flag.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Retry on 5xx but not on 4xx: what about 408/429?" → Retry 408/429 (honor Retry-After) and 502/503/504; do not retry 500 for non-idempotent calls; never retry 400/401/403/404/409/422 (401 is handled by the authenticator, not by retry).
  • "How do you test backoff?" → Inject Random and use runTest virtual time; assert delays stay within [0, cap], and that the total attempt count and budget decrement match.
  • "A Flow that should retry on failure?" → retryWhen { cause, attempt -> ... delay(...); cause.isRetryable() && attempt < 3 } — note retry/retryWhen only see upstream exceptions, and they do not catch CancellationException from the collector's cancellation (downstream cancellation is not an upstream error).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a brownout in which retries amplified load, the postmortem's highest-leverage action was not the breaker but the retry budget: it cost 40 lines and capped the amplification at about 1.1x. The breaker came later and mostly improved UX (instant cached fallback instead of a spinner).
